content:
The Great Rate Escape: Examining the Impact of Rising Interest Rates on Your Fixed Deposit Aspirations
While investing in a [fixed deposit](https://altifi.ai/), investors usually
feel safe, secure, and assured about returns. And that’s true. Fixed deposits
have long been a bankable investment avenue, especially for those looking to
earn a steady periodic interest and safeguard their principal amount. However,
did you know, fixed deposit interest rates fluctuate and whether rising or
declining, they can affect your fixed deposit returns? Yes! So, let’s examine a
few aspects of changing interest rates on your fixed deposit returns. 
What is a Fixed Deposit?
Most of you would already know what fixed deposits are. However, for
those who are new to the world of [fixed deposits](https://altifi.ai/sign_up), here’s an overview of what
fixed deposits are. So, [fixed deposits](https://altifi.ai/) are a financial
instrument usually offered by banks and other financial institutions. They
require depositors to invest a specific amount for a particular duration
(ranging from seven days to ten years) and at a predetermined interest rate.
Accordingly, some also address fixed deposits as term deposits.
Some essential features of a fixed deposit include fixed interest rates, fixed tenure, periodic interest payments (monthly, quarterly, or yearly as chosen by the depositor), return of principal upon maturity, liquidity, and safety.
Fixed interest rates may excite many. However, what if there’s a change
in the [interest rates](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) due to inflation, the country’s economic policy, or any
other reason? That’s something everyone should consider before opening a fixed
deposit. Here’s more to it.
The Role of Interest Rates in Fixed Deposits
Fixed deposits usually offer guaranteed returns. However, their interest
rates change over a while and impact fixed deposit returns. Rising interest
rates can increase fixed deposits. On the other hand, a decline in the interest
rates affects the returns adversely. But why do banks revise fixed deposit
rates and which factors impact fixed deposit [interest rates](https://altifi.ai/)? Here’s the answer.
Why Banks Revise Fixed Deposit Rates?
Banks operate as part of the broader economic landscape of a country. Hence, the fixed deposit returns they offer aren’t devoid of external economic circumstances and factors like the repo rate of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Hence, banks revised fixed deposit interest rates regularly to keep up with the existing market conditions.
Speaking of the repo rate, RBI reviews it periodically and makes changes to it. The repo rate has a direct relation with your fixed deposit interest rate.

content:
ence, the fixed deposit returns they offer aren’t devoid of external economic circumstances and factors like the repo rate of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Hence, banks revised fixed deposit interest rates regularly to keep up with the existing market conditions.
Speaking of the repo rate, RBI reviews it periodically and makes changes to it. The repo rate has a direct relation with your fixed deposit interest rate. Hence, changes to the repo rate can impact the latter, no matter whether it is a bank or a NBFC fixed deposit.
The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets the repo rate that serves as a benchmark interest rate. The repo rate impacts the cost of borrowing to banks and that affects various financial markets, including fixed deposits. MPC sets the repo rate based on its evaluation of inflation and other economic factors. Inflation affects savings interest rates, including fixed deposits and the purchasing power of the returns investors earn on them. It determines the investment’s real value over time and the amount one would pay for a fixed deposit compared to its inflation-adjusted value in cash.
Apart from repo rates, banks revise fixed deposit interest rates based on inflation and competition with other financial institutions. Let’s look at the various factors influencing the interest rates of fixed deposits.
Factors Impacting Interest Rates
Here are some factors that significantly drive interest rates.
A Country’s Economic Condition
Interest rates increase amidst a flourishing economy due to an increase in demand for credit. However, amidst a floundering economy, interest rates fall to trigger borrowing and spending. In the latter situation, fixed deposit returns are likely to reduce.
Central Bank Policy
Another vital aspect with a say in a country’s fixed deposit interest rates is the country’s bank. The bank has the power to increase or decrease interest rates to control inflation and foster economic growth within the country.
Inflation Rate
As we mentioned a couple of times earlier, inflation also has a critical impact on interest rates. High inflation causes lenders to charge higher interest rates to compensate for the reduced purchasing power of the money they provide.
Government Policies
Government policies are as crucial in fixed deposit interest rates as they are in other areas. Tax reductions or increased spending can impact interest rates. For example, if the government increases its expenditures, it can scale up the demand for credit and cause the interest rates as well to increase.
Repo Rate
With a repo rate reduction, banks may reduce their fixed deposit interest rates to promote lending and economic growth. On the other hand, if the repo rate increases, banks may increase their fixed deposit interest rates to call upon more deposits.
Global Economic Situation
The world is an economically small place where one country’s economic
crisis can impact another country’s economy. And when economic downwaves like
recession grip a country, they can [impact](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) its interest rates negatively.

title: Are Fixed Deposits Still Worth It? Comparing FDs With Bonds
content:
Global Economic Situation
The world is an economically small place where one country’s economic
crisis can impact another country’s economy. And when economic downwaves like
recession grip a country, they can [impact](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) its interest rates negatively. 
How do Interest Rate Changes Affect Fixed Deposit Returns?
While you’ve now seen some of the vital factors responsible for changes in interest rates, let’s see how changing interest rates affect fixed deposit returns.
Increase in Returns with Higher Interest Rates: Higher interest rates
increase fixed deposit [returns](https://altifi.ai/sign_up), making the latter a more attractive investment
avenue.
Negative Effect of Inflation: High inflation is bad for every economy. While reducing people’s spending capacity, it can cause a noteworthy reduction in the actual returns of a fixed deposit. If inflation rates surpass the interest rate of the fixed deposit, it is evident that the actual value of the investment will also erode.
Fund Lock-In Opportunity Cost: A rise in the interest rates makes fixed deposits more lucrative. However, such fixed deposits come at a cost. They require you to lock in your funds for a particular period. Such terms and conditions can compel you to compromise your investment aspirations. You wouldn’t be able to leverage other investment options amidst rising interest rates, as you would have already locked a significant amount of your funds in a fixed deposit.
Impact on Longer Tenure Fixed Deposits: Fixed deposits invested for a longer time remain exposed to interest rate changes for a longer time. Hence, they are more affected than those with shorter tenures.
Effect on Reinvestment: Often, people keep reinvesting their fixed deposit at maturity. However, interest rate variations can impact the returns on reinvestment. For example, if the interest rate at the time of reinvestment is lower than earlier, reinvesting the fixed deposit amount will yield lower returns.
Why Different Institutions Have Varying Fixed Deposit Interest Rates?
Fixed deposit interest rates depend on the bank or the financial institution's ability to repay the fixed deposit. You can measure a financial organization's financial health by its capital level. For instance, a high capital level signifies abundant funds to compensate for losses and maintain lower operational costs. The fixed deposit rate denotes the institution’s financial muscle.
How to Deal with Fixed Deposit Interest Rate Changes?
An increase in fixed deposit interest rates applies to all tenures. Long-term fixed deposits are affected more than their shorter counterparts. Amidst high-interest rates and increasing inflations, one may consider opening a short-term fixed deposit. Once the inflation settles, they can go for a long-term fixed deposit.
Besides, you can split a large deposit into smaller fragments deposited for varying tenures to get the periodic liquidity and interest rate volatility advantage.

title: Beat Inflation in India (2024): Go Beyond Fixed Deposits with Strategic Bonds
content:
Feeling Anxious About Inflation? Tame the Heat with the Right Bond Strategy
Inflation is something that worries everyone. Believe it or not, even the richest of all dread the rising inflation rates! So, feeling anxious about it is usual. In India, inflation has long been a hot political and economic issue. The government has been able to control it significantly in recent years. However, it would be unrealistic to expect it to remain constant throughout and at the same time, enjoy historic economic growth.
India’s current [inflation](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) rate stands at 5.69 per cent (as
of December 2023), which marks a 1.6 per cent decline compared to 2022, when it
was 6.7 per cent. Although that’s great news for now, in the long run, you
should be prepared to tackle the rising inflation mercury with the right
investment strategy. Are [bond
investments](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) one? Let’s find it out.
The Relation Between Inflation and Economic Growth
India is one of the fastest-growing economies in the world and is also projected to soon become one of the top five. Nonetheless, what’s worth remembering here is that we live in a growing economy. We offer a flourishing environment for every business, no matter IT, healthcare, manufacturing or hospitality. There’s something for everyone in India.
Inflation rates and gross demand product (GDP)
(a significant part of every economy) are closely related. [Inflation](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) can rise with GDP growth driven
by augmented demand or a drop in supply. A balanced relationship can help
prevent a considerable rise in inflation.
A growing GDP with a trivial increase in the associated inflation indicates a healthy economy and a progressive nation. It refers to companies producing goods, earning profits, employing people and paying wages regularly. On the other hand, it also signifies a considerable increase in demand and consumer spending capacity.
While a rise in the GDP proves exciting, it is worth noting that excessive GDP growth can shoot the inflation rate, impact businesses and cause consumer spending to plummet.
Although we are part of the macroeconomic
environment, individually, we cannot do much to control it. Besides, a
country’s economy also depends on the global economic weather. Economic down
waves or geopolitical vagaries across other countries can impact our economy
and inflation rates as well. So, how do you keep up with the inflation
fluctuations or increments at your level? Of course, it is through smart and
futuristic investments. Let’s examine a few of them, including [bonds](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) in this regard.

With economic growth, inflation, although at varying rates, is inevitable. So, let’s talk about solutions instead of problems.
Inflation grows over a period. In unstable or floundering economies, it might skyrocket at any given point. Again, it also offers investment avenues that can help investors keep up with the growing inflation graph. Bonds are one of them. But are they good enough? And if so, what type of bonds can prove potentially remunerative to stay afloat?

Floating bonds adjust their interest rates
periodically and therefore, present a more agile and flexible approach to the
dynamic economic environment of a country. Thus, investing in [floating rate bonds](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) ensures that your
returns remain aligned with the changing market conditions, serving as a hedge
against the potential economic damage inflation may cause to your investments
and returns.

These bonds align their both interest payments and principal according to the
Consumer Price Index (CPI). Thus, by aligning with inflation rates, IIBs help
preserve your investment’s real value. They also provide a reliable investment
for everyone looking for portfolio protection against inflation.

Short-term bonds are another effective way to decrease inflation sensitivity. These bonds have shorter maturity periods. content:
According to the World Gold Council, India's gold demand surged by approximately 8% year-on-year to 136.6 tonnes in the April quarter of 2026, fuelled by a strong economic environment despite record-high prices. This shows the deep-rooted reverence Indians tend to have for gold as a symbol of wealth and financial security. However, if an individual wishes to invest in gold without the worry of storage and security, the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) can be a secure alternative to traditional gold investments. To know more about SGB benefits, keep reading on.
What are Sovereign Gold Bonds?
[Sovereign Gold Bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/sovereign-gold-bond) are debt securities backed by the government and issued by the Reserve Bank of India. With SGBs, investors can invest in gold without the hassle of physically owning it. SGBs are denominated in grams of gold.
SGBs and physical gold are similar in numerous ways. When an individual sells gold, they can benefit from the potential rise in gold prices. Similarly, individuals can benefit from any potential capital appreciation when their SGBs mature. The additional benefit of SGBs is that investors can earn fixed interest, typically paid semi-annually.
In the case of SGBs, investors are essentially investing in gold while not having to worry about the cons associated with owning it physically, i.e., storage and theft. Individuals as well as institutional investors can hold SGBs in physical or Demat form. These bonds have a maturity of 8 years; however, investors can choose to exit after 5 years.
The minimum an investor or any entity can invest in SGBs is 1 gram of gold. As an individual or member of Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs), the maximum gold one can purchase this way is 4 kg in a fiscal year. Trusts and other similar entities can buy up to 20 kg in a year.
Typically, the RBI issues SGBs in tranches throughout the year, based on a predetermined schedule. Each tranche has a specific issue date and subscription window. Investors can get information on the issue dates by checking notifications from the RBI website, banks, post offices, stock exchanges or online investment platforms like Altifi.
Benefits of SGBs
SGBs have certain benefits over physical gold. Below mentioned are their inherent advantages:
Fixed Interest Rate
Sovereign Gold Bonds offer fixed interest rates. Currently, SGBs provide a 2.5% per annum interest on the initial investment amount. This interest is paid to investors semi-annually. This interest is an additional benefit over the potential capital appreciation of gold itself.

title: What Are the Benefits of Sovereign Gold Bonds?
content:
SGBs have certain benefits over physical gold. Below mentioned are their inherent advantages:
Fixed Interest Rate
Sovereign Gold Bonds offer fixed interest rates. Currently, SGBs provide a 2.5% per annum interest on the initial investment amount. This interest is paid to investors semi-annually. This interest is an additional benefit over the potential capital appreciation of gold itself. Note that the interest earned is taxable per the Income Tax Act, 1961.
Capital Appreciation Potential
SGBs are directly linked to the prevailing market price of gold. Given the historical trend of gold prices, especially during economic downturns, gold has typically been seen as a hedge against inflation and market volatility. With SGBs, individuals may benefit from the capital appreciation of gold over time.
Tax Benefits
Sovereign Gold Bonds come with multiple tax advantages that may make them a compelling investment. If held until maturity, i.e., 8 years, the capital gains from the appreciation of the gold price are exempt from tax.
No Tax Deducted at Source (TDS)
These bonds are exempt from TDS. The absence of TDS ensures that individuals can maximise their interest earnings, leading to higher overall returns from their SGB investments.
Backed by the Government
The most significant advantage of Sovereign Gold Bonds is that they provide is their government backing. Since SGBs are issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India, the investment comes with a sovereign guarantee. This ensures that investors’ both capital and interest are secure.
Liquidity and Tradability
Sovereign Gold Bonds are highly liquid, and investors can trade them on the stock exchanges. This way, investors can easily buy and sell their holdings. This liquidity ensures that if investors need to exit their investment before maturity, they have the option to do so with ease. Moreover, SGBs offer an additional liquidity option through premature redemption after five years, with payouts based on the prevailing gold prices.
Transferability
Individuals can gift or transfer SGBs to a relative, friend, or anyone who meets the eligibility criteria. To do this before maturity, investors need to follow the transfer process as outlined in the Government Securities Act 2006 and the Government Securities Regulations 2007. All an individual needs to do is complete the transfer using an instrument of transfer which is available through the issuing agents.
Pledge as Collateral
Another advantage of the Sovereign Gold Bond is that investors may get a loan against it. Investors can use these securities as collateral for loans from banks, financial institutions, and Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs). The Loan to Value (LTV) ratio will be the same as that applied to regular gold loans, as prescribed by the RBI from time to time.

The following are some aspects that investors may consider before investing in Sovereign Gold Bonds:
- SGBs are issued by the Reserve Bank of India on behalf of the Government of India, thereby ensuring high credibility as opposed to other financial tools.
- They come with a predefined interest rate of about 2.5%, which is provided at regular intervals in addition to potential price appreciation.
- Returns are linked to the market price of gold, which means the overall value may rise or fall depending on price movements.
- Under the revised tax rules effective April 1, 2026, capital gains on Sovereign Gold Bonds will be tax-free only if the bonds are purchased during the original issue and held until full 8-year maturity. Any early exit, including redemption after 5 years or sale before maturity, will be treated as a premature exit and subject to capital gains tax.
- These securities have a limited issuance throughout the year, meaning that availability will generally depend on their issuance cycle.
- While they are listed on stock exchanges, liquidity in the secondary market may vary and may not always support an easy exit.
- There will generally be no taxes charged on capital gain at the end of the maturity. However, the interest is subject to income taxes, as per applicable income tax rules.
- Since SGBs are held in electronic form, there is generally no concern related to storage, safety, or gold purity.
- SGBs can also be used as collateral for loans.
- SGBs are normally preferred by investors who have a long-term investment objective.
Eligibility Criteria for SGB
The following entities can purchase SGBs:
- Resident individuals
- Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs)
- Trusts
- Universities
- Charitable trusts
If an investor is a Non-Resident Indian (NRI), they are not eligible to invest in new SGBs. However, if the investor were an Indian resident when they bought the SGBs, they can continue to hold them even after the change in residence.

content:
Bond Basics: 5 Essential Concepts Every Investor Should Grasp
Are you looking to earn steady and sustainable returns on your interests? Then, you may consider investing in bonds. However, bond investments have some basic concepts that every investor should know and comprehend before investing. It will help them make an informed and prudent investment decision. So, from the basic definition of bonds to their advantages and disadvantages, here are five essential concepts of bonds every investor should learn while investing money in any bond type.
Bond – Definition and Types
A bond is an investment instrument, essentially a type of loan the bond issuer (usually a company or government) borrows from the investor or bondholder. a loan made by an investor to a borrower. In other words, the investor lends money to the issuer for a particular period. During this period, the issuer agrees to make periodic interest payments, termed coupon payments and repay the bond’s face value, called principal at the bond’s maturity date. Companies or governments usually issue bonds to fund their projects, finance equipment purchases, expand geographically, etc.
Bonds are offered in various types. Some of them include the following.
- Government Bonds: As the name suggests, governments issue bonds to fund public projects. Some types of government bonds include treasury bonds and municipal bonds. Government bonds are usually considered safer as they are backed by the trust and stability of the respective government.
- Corporate Bonds: Again, as the name indicates, these bonds are issued by companies to finance their expansion plans, operations, project completions, etc.
- Convertible Bonds: Another significant bond type includes the convertible bond. It is a fixed-income debt security that pays interest. However, it can be converted into common stock or equity shares.
- Zero-Coupon Bonds: Zero-coupons do not pay periodic interest. However, they are sold at a discount to their face value and redeemed at face value on maturity. It is the difference between the purchase price and the face value that signifies the interest the bondholder has earned.
- Callable Bonds: Callable bonds allow the issuer to redeem the bond before maturity but typically after a specified period. The facility to call the bond benefits issuers in situations wherein there’s an interest rate decline. It allows them to refinance at a lower rate. But in such cases, investors confront a loss!
- Perpetual Bonds: These bonds do not have a maturity date and pay interest to bondholders indefinitely.
- Green Bonds: The word green itself indicates that these bonds fund climate and environmental projects. Hence, they are popular among sustainable investors.
Essential Components of Bonds
A few general and fundamental components of bonds include the following.
- Principal/Par Value: It is the initial amount of money the investor lends to the issuer, usually paid at the bond’s maturity.

A few general and fundamental components of bonds include the following.

- Coupon Payments: Coupon payments are periodic interest payments the issuer makes to the bondholders.

- Price: Price is the market value at which the bond is bought or sold. These can vary depending on interest rates, credit quality, etc.
- Yield: It is the effective annual return on the bond, considering coupon payments and the bond's price. The yield usually drives the investment appeal of a bond investment.
- Credit Rating: It denotes the issuer’s creditworthiness and its default likelihood. Credit ratings are provided by various credit rating agencies worldwide.
Calculation of Bond Yields
A bond yield refers to the expected returns over a period and any fixed income an investor would earn upon investing in a particular bond. Bond yield considers future cash flows and provides the rate of return. It is expressed as a percentage depending upon the market investment amount. One can calculate the bond yield tenure monthly, quarterly or annually. Bond yield is calculated based on the coupon payment dividing the coupon payment by the bond’s purchase price. However, it should be noted that there are different types of bond yields. Let’s look at an example.
If you purchased a bond for Rs. 5,000 and received Rs. 500 as the annual coupon payment, the bond yield was Rs. 500/Rs. 5,000 = 0.1, ten per cent annual rate. The most widely used bond yield calculation is the coupon payment divided by the bond’s face value. Thus, coupon rate = annual interest payment/bond face value.
The bond’s coupon rate is the interest rate the bond carries on its face value and not the market value. However, if the bond trades at a premium or discount, the bond yield rate will differ from the coupon rate as the bond yield is determined based on its purchase value.

Identifying the Right Bonds
Bonds demand a considerable investment. Hence, you should make a wise and informed decision after carefully considering a range of factors, including the following.
- Yield: Higher yields often come with higher risk. Hence, you should consider consulting an expert before choosing a bond based on its yield offering.
- Interest Rate Risk: Comprehend how interest rate variations can affect bond prices. Bond prices usually fall when interest rates rise and vice versa.
- Duration: The bond’s duration calculates its sensitivity to interest rate variations. Longer-duration bonds are more sensitive to rate changes. Hence, they are riskier when it comes to interest rates.
- Liquidity: Liquidity is another significant concern. You should determine how straightforward it is to buy or sell the bond in the secondary market. Bonds with less liquidity may have broader bid-ask spreads. Bondholders may find it more challenging to sell such bonds without keeping the price unperturbed.
- Issuer Risk: The issuer’s credibility, financial health and stability also matter while making a bond investment. Usually, government bonds are considered safer than corporate bonds. However, that’s a general consideration. You should mandatorily check the risk level of a particular bond investment, no matter the issuer.
- Fees and Expenses: Know the fees or expenses associated with buying, holding or selling a particular bond. Factor in these costs in your returns to calculate the latter more accurately.
- Tax Considerations: In some bonds, the income earned through the interest rate is taxable per the Income Tax Act, 1961. Hence, ensure you also understand the tax implications before you invest in a particular bond.
- Credit Ratings: In addition to the issuer risk, also evaluate the issuer’s creditworthiness through its credit ratings. It will help you determine the default risk and essentially the reliability of the bond investment.
- Economic Environment: Make it a point to also assess the current economic environment and its impact on interest rates, bond performance, etc.
Pros and Cons of Investing in Bonds
Like every other investment platform, investing in bonds also comes with a few advantages and disadvantages. Some general ones include the following.
Advantages:
- Predictable Returns: Bonds are fixed-income securities that generate predictable returns, especially when you hold them until maturity. They also pay interest regularly, thereby providing steady income to investors.
- Capital Preservation: Usually, people consider bonds less risky than stocks. Hence, they form a prudent choice for capital preservation.
- Diversification: Investors can also diversify their investments and spread the risk across various asset classes by investing in bonds.
- Liquidity: Investors can buy and sell bonds easily in the secondary market. That refers to liquidity.
Disadvantages:
- Interest Rate Risk: Bond prices and interest rates have an inverse relationship.

title: Bond: A Not-So-Secret Agent in Your Investment Portfolio
content:
We’re living in a digital era, where everybody is quick to hop onto the bandwagon of trends. One such trend that has recently caught on is investing. Now when we say investing, the first thought in your mind might just be investing in the stock markets. This could be a result of the frequent announcements of IPOs, Mutual Fund NFOs, or the growing presence of trading platforms. However, ‘Bonds as an alternative investment option remain an underdog.
Now the next logical question to pop in your mind would be - what are bonds exactly, and why have they been in the shadows, right?
Just as we borrow money for various needs, an organization may also borrow funds to fulfil its financial needs for various purposes such as expansion, infrastructure development, working capital requirements, etc. The organization can do so by issuing bonds (becoming the issuer) to seek interested investors (the lenders).
You may wonder - what’s in it for the investor?
In return for the investment made by the investor, the issuer shall then add an interest amount over the principal amount invested. These interest payments are usually fixed in nature and follow a predetermined schedule. Thus, bonds are also commonly known as fixed-income instruments.
So why are bonds still alien to us?
It’s mainly because bonds as investment instruments were only accessible to HNIs (High Net-worth Individuals) due to their high-ticket size (i.e. the minimum investment amount was very high). However, in recent years, bonds have been made accessible to the masses by facilitating investment through small ticket sizes (even as low as a hundred rupees).
Now that we know what bonds are, let’s understand how they differ from our go-to investment avenues such as mutual funds or stocks.
We all have heard stories of people who invested in equity and received massive returns, sometimes overnight too. While that may be the case, equity markets are volatile and can go on a downward track. Due to such market risks, investments can lose their value, denoting high-risk and high-reward situations.
This is how bonds are different; they help you diversify risk in your portfolio and are less volatile than equity. However, one needs to be careful while investing in bonds as if the issuer company runs into trouble, they could default on their obligations and investors can face losses. It is therefore important to do a diligence of the issuer and understand the risks of the product before investing in any security, be it bonds or equity.
In a nutshell, below are a few characteristics of investing in bonds.
- Fixed-income stream
- Diversification from equity and bank deposits
- Lower risk than stocks of the issuing company

Bond Investment Strategies: 5 Approaches to Enhance Your Financial Goals
Are you a novice investor toying with the idea of investing in [bonds](https://altifi.ai/) or have recently begun your bond journey and want to make the most from your investment decision? Well, investing in bonds may appear pretty straightforward. Buy a reliable bond and earn returns. However, we only wish it was as simple. This is because the purpose of investing in bonds is to receive optimal returns across a wider time frame. Achieving these objectives is more likely when you have the right investment strategy. Accordingly, let’s look at five approaches or [investment strategies](https://altifi.ai/) to enhance your financial goals.
What is a Bond?
A bond is a popular investment instrument across the investment market. It is a financial instrument that denotes a loan a company or a government (bond issuer) borrows from an investor (bondholder). Thus, when an investor invests in a bond, they lend money to the bond issuer in exchange for a periodic interest payment and principal repayment. The Indian market offers various types of bonds and each bond has different components associated with it. Some common ones include the following.
- Issuer: It is the company or government that issues the bond and commits to make period interest payments and the principal amount upon maturity.
- Maturity Date: It is the date when the issuer of the bond will repay the bond's face value to the bondholder.
- Face Value: The Face Value is the amount the bondholder will receive from the issuer upon the bond’s maturity.
- Coupon Rate: It is the interest rate the issuer agrees to pay the bondholder. The amount is usually denoted as a percentage of the bond's face value. Bond issuers generally pay interest annually or semi-annually.
- Bond Rating: Bond rating signifies the creditworthiness of a bond. Credit rating agencies provide these ratings based on their assessment and analysis of various factors related to the issuer. The bond rating does not guarantee returns. However, it helps investors make informed investment decisions.
How Do Bonds Generate Returns?
When the issuer issues a bond, they borrow money from the investor. In return, they commit to pay interest for the bond’s tenure and return the principal amount upon maturity. The issuers inform aspects like tenure, maturity date, interest rate, etc., while issuing the bond. The annual returns the bond investor can expect to earn if they hold the bond until maturity is denoted by yield to maturity (YTM). Bond returns essentially have two significant elements. They include the following.
Periodic Interest Payments:
This is the most lucrative part of a bond investment. Investors buy bonds to receive periodic interest payments either annually or semi-annually. That refers to creating a steady and predictable source of income.

title: Bond Investment Strategies | Altifi - a bond investment platform
content:
Bond laddering is a complex yet popular strategy that requires you to break your amount and invest it into various bonds of multiple tenures. For instance, if you have Rs. 2,00,000, you would divide the amount into five parts and invest it in five different bonds with varying tenures like two years, three years, five years and so on.
Now, when each bond matures, reinvest the amount into the bond with the longest maturity period. Accordingly, you will have a bond that matures every year (spacing) and gets reinvested in a five-year bond at potentially varying yields. Making this strategy effective requires you to split your total investment equally and maintain as equal spacing as possible. The bond should mature after a particular number of years.
The fundamental purpose of investing in a bond ladder strategy is to avoid locking your money in a low bond yield. Let’s say you buy a bond for five years at seven per cent interest and invest all your money into it. The next year, the issuer issues a five-year bond at eight per cent yield due to market changes. In such a situation, the price of your five-year bond will reduce, and you will earn a one per cent lower yield.
If you had split your money into five parts, you would have invested 20 per cent of it in a five-year bond with seven per cent interest. Furthermore, another 20 per cent of the amount you invested in a one-year bond would have been reinvested into a five-year bond at a higher yield of one per cent after the maturity of the one-year bond.
What if the bond yield drops down to four or five per cent instead of increasing to eight per cent after a year? In that case, you would have a five-year bond with seven per cent.
Hold to Maturity (HTM) Strategy:
It is one of the most straightforward bond investment strategies. As the name suggests, the strategy requires you to invest in bonds and hold them until maturity without making any withdrawals. In such a situation, the price of your five-year bond will reduce, and you will earn a one per cent lower yield.
If you had split your money into five parts, you would have invested 20 per cent of it in a five-year bond with seven per cent interest. Did you know that bonds can also have Initial Public Offerings (IPOs)? With the growing demand for low-risk investment options, Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) have become a popular choice for investors seeking stable income. In India, NCD IPOs are now emerging as an accessible and reliable fixed-income avenue for retail and institutional investors alike.
The Indian corporate bond market has experienced consistent growth, with a CAGR of ~9% over the past five years. Analysts project that the market could surpass INR 100–120 lakh crore by 2030, further expanding opportunities for investors through NCDs and other structured debt instruments.
Key Takeaways
- NCD IPOs provide fixed returns and stable income, making them ideal for conservative investors.
- With a minimum investment as low as INR 1,000, NCD IPOs are accessible to a wide range of investors.
- Regulated by SEBI and listed on NSE/BSE, NCD IPOs ensure transparency, credibility, and secure investment tracking.
- They help diversify portfolios by reducing exposure to equity market volatility.
- Platforms
 like [Altifi.ai](https://altifi.ai/bonds/ncd-ipo) offer features such as Sell Bonds Anytime, enhancing liquidity and
 investor flexibility.
What Are NCD Bond IPOs?
A Non-Convertible Debenture (NCD) IPO is a public issuance of debt securities by a company to raise capital from investors. Unlike convertible debentures, NCDs cannot be converted into equity, and investors earn fixed interest (coupon) payments at regular intervals. At maturity, the principal is repaid in full, providing predictable returns.
NCDs are suitable for investors looking for a steady income stream without exposure to market volatility. They are issued in multiple tenures, ranging from short-term (1–3 years) to long-term (up to 10 years or more), catering to various financial goals.
Benefits of Investing in NCD IPOs
- Predictable
 Fixed Income
NCDs offer fixed coupon rates for the entire tenure, enabling investors to plan their cash flows effectively.
- Low
 Minimum Investment
Most NCD IPOs require as little as INR 1,000, making them accessible for first-time and small investors.
- Regulated
 and Transparent
SEBI regulates NCD IPOs, ensuring strict adherence to guidelines, disclosure norms, and investor protection measures.
- Listed
 on Stock Exchanges
NCDs are credited to the investor’s demat account and listed on NSE/BSE, allowing easy tracking and future trading.
- Portfolio
 Diversification
NCDs are fixed-income instruments that reduce portfolio risk, complementing equities and mutual funds.
- Lower
 Risk Compared to Stocks

Tax-Efficient Investing: Leveraging Bonds for Better Returns and Lower Liabilities
[Bonds](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) can form a prudent investment
choice, especially for those looking to create a steady source of income.
However, most bonds aren’t tax-free. The periodic interest you earn on them is
taxable. So, taxes can eat up a significant portion of your returns!
Nevertheless, not all bond investments are taxable. Thanks to the Indian
investment horizon, you can choose from a range of tax-efficient bonds to curb
or eliminate the tax impact. Thus, if you also endeavour to make a
tax-efficient investment, here’s a blog you shouldn’t miss reading.
What is a Tax-Free Bond?
[Tax-free bonds](https://altifi.ai/sign_up), like other bonds, are
debt instruments that the Indian government or its authorised entities like
public sector undertakings (PSU) and infrastructure companies issue to call
upon investments. As the name suggests, these bonds offer tax-free interest income.
So, that means the interest you earn on such bonds is not subject to income tax
deductions in India.
Types of Tax-Free Bonds
Since tax-free bonds are issued by government-related organisations, some common types of tax-free bonds, based on the issuer, include the following.
- Power Bonds: Power generation companies looking for operational expansion or requiring funds to maintain power plans issue these bonds.
- Infrastructure Bonds: Infrastructure companies building airports, roads, etc., issue these bonds to fetch finance for large-scale projects.
- Public Sector Unit Bonds: Government-owned entities or organisations like HUDCO, NTPC, NHAI, REC, PFC, etc., issue these bonds to fund infrastructure, power, and housing projects.
- Railway Bonds: As the name suggests, the issuer of these bonds is the Indian Railways. The objective of gathering money through these bonds is to finance the expansion and modernisation of the Indian railway network.
- Housing Bonds: Entities like the National Housing Bank issue these bonds to finance economical housing projects across the country.
Features of Tax-Free Bonds
Tax-free bonds form a potentially lucrative proposition for the following reasons that also constitute their features.
- Tax Exemption: The foremost
advantage or feature of tax-free bonds is that the income you earn from these
bonds is exempt from income tax. So, if you are looking to potentially maximise
[returns](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) and minimise your tax liabilities, you
may choose to invest in tax-free bonds.
- Fixed But Higher
Interest Rate: Tax-free bonds have a fixed rate. However, it is
higher than many other regular [fixed-incomeinstruments](https://altifi.ai/sign_up). Usually, the annual interest rate can range between 5.50 and
7.50 per cent.

title: Bonds vs Debentures: Key Differences & Investment Insights
content:
The comparison between bonds and debentures shows how governments and companies use fixed income instruments to raise funds from investors. Bond investments provide safer returns because they receive government protection whereas debenture investments deliver greater potential returns, but users face increased investment risk. The process of evaluating their definitions, operational mechanisms, essential dissimilarities, associated dangers, tax regulations, and investment suitability for various skills levels enables both novice and expert investors to make better financial choices.
What is a Bond?
A bond is a fixed income investment which requires you to lend money to an issuer and receive interest payments until the bond reaches maturity. At the bond maturity date, you will receive all your original investment back to you.
The government and public sector companies and private organisations in India issue bonds to the public. People consider government bonds, which are known as G-Secs, to be the safest investment option because these bonds receive complete government protection.
Bonds pay interest to their investors through predetermined payment schedules which occur twice a year or once a year. Investors who want to earn stable income with minimal danger from market fluctuations select these investments because they provide steady results.
Key Features of Bonds
- Issued by governments, PSUs, and corporations
- Often backed by assets or government guarantee
- Offer fixed or floating interest payments
- Long tenures, ranging from 1 to 40 years
- Rated by agencies like CRISIL and ICRA
- Can be bought and sold on stock exchanges
Types of Bonds
Different types of bonds are:
- Government Bonds (G-Secs): These bonds are safe and secure and offer a guarantee from the government.
- Corporate Bonds: These bonds offer higher returns but involve a risk factor.
- Municipal Bonds: These bonds are issued to raise funds for local infrastructure projects.
- Tax-Free Bonds: The interest that is earned on these bonds is tax-free.
- Infrastructure Bonds: These bonds help raise funds for infrastructure projects.
- Zero Coupon Bonds: These bonds are issued at a discount and can be redeemed at face value.
What is a Debenture?
A debenture is a type of debt instrument issued by companies to raise funds. In many cases, it is not backed by specific assets, which means it depends on the company’s financial strength.
In India, Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) are the most common type. The instruments provide fixed returns which investors cannot exchange for company stock. The instruments are under SEBI regulation, and they function as a common industry standard.
Debentures usually offer higher interest rates than bonds. The reason is that unsecured debt securities present greater risk to investors.
Key Features of Debentures
The key features of debentures are as follows.
- Issued only by companies
- Can be secured or unsecured
- Offer fixed and often higher returns
- May be convertible into shares

title: Bonds vs Debentures: Key Differences & Investment Insights
content:
Debentures usually offer higher interest rates than bonds. The reason is that unsecured debt securities present greater risk to investors.
Key Features of Debentures
The key features of debentures are as follows.
- Issued only by companies
- Can be secured or unsecured
- Offer fixed and often higher returns
- May be convertible into shares
- Require mandatory credit ratings
- Regulated by SEBI
Types of Debentures
The types of debentures include:
- Secured Debentures: Backed by company assets
- Unsecured Debentures: No collateral, higher risk
- Convertible Debentures: Can be converted into equity
- Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs): Fixed returns, no conversion
- Redeemable Debentures: Repaid after a fixed period
- Perpetual Debentures: No fixed maturity, rare in India
Key Differences Between Bonds and Debentures
The difference between debentures and bonds are as follows.
| Parameter | Bonds | Debentures | 
| Issuer | Government, PSUs, corporations | Companies only | 
| Security | Usually secured or guaranteed | May or may not be secured | 
| Risk | Lower | Moderate to high | 
| Returns | Stable but lower | Higher | 
| Regulation | RBI and SEBI | SEBI | 
| Convertibility | Not convertible | May be convertible | 
| Collateral | Often present | Not always | 
| Priority | Higher in repayment | Lower than secured bonds | 
| Credit Rating | Required (corporate) | Mandatory | 
| Tenure | 1–40 years | Usually 1–10 years | 
Note: In practice, the credit rating and the issuer’s strength matter more than the label itself.
Risk Comparison: Bonds vs Debentures
Credit Risk
Government bonds are highly reliable and carry very low risk. Debentures depend on the company’s financial health. Ratings from AAA to D help investors assess this risk.
Interest Rate Risk
When interest rates rise, prices of existing bonds and debentures fall. This matters if you plan to sell before maturity.
Liquidity Risk
Government bonds and highly rated NCDs are easier to sell. Smaller or less popular issues may not raise interest among buyers easily.
Inflation Risk
If inflation rises above the return rate, your real earnings reduce. This is important in today’s changing market conditions.
Who Should Invest in Bonds vs Debentures?
Here's who may consider investing in bonds and debentures.
- Conservative Investors: Prefer government bonds for safety and steady income
- Moderate Investors: Choose high-rated corporate bonds or secured NCDs
- Higher-risk Investors: Consider lower-rated debentures for better returns

- Understand the tax impact

Bonds are usually safer and may be backed by assets or the government, while debentures depend more on company strength.

Mostly yes, especially government bonds. But highly rated debentures can also be reliable.

An NCD is a Non-Convertible Debenture that offers fixed returns and cannot be converted into shares.

Yes, both provide interest payments at regular intervals.
5. Which is better for beginners?
Bonds are generally easier and safer for first-time investors.

Yes, if they are listed on exchanges, they can be sold before maturity.

title: Bonds Vs Fixed Deposit | AltiFi
content:
Introduction
When investing,
many pursue stability and predictable returns, making Bonds and Fixed Deposits
(FDs) popular choices. Both are relatively low-risk investments that provide
steady income. However, they differ notably in terms of returns, liquidity and
investment strategies. Bonds may offer predictable returns with varying risk
profiles and liquidity, while FDs provide assured returns with fixed interest
rates and limited liquidity. The detailed [differences between Bonds and FDs](https://altifi.ai/bonds) are
outlined below.
What are Bonds?
Bonds are debt
securities issued by governments or corporations to raise funds. When you buy a
bond, you are lending money to the issuer in return for periodic interest
payments and the repayment of the principal amount at maturity. Bonds can vary
in terms of duration, interest rates and risk profiles, depending on the
issuer’s creditworthiness and the bond’s specific features. This diversity
allows you to choose bonds that align with your risk tolerance and investment
goals.
Types of Bonds
Bonds are broadly categorized into the following types:
• Government Bonds: Issued by central or state governments, these bonds are considered relatively low-risk as they are backed by the government’s credit. Examples include Dated Government Securities (G-Secs), Treasury Bills (T-Bills), Cash Management Bills (CMBs) and State Development Loans (SDLs).
• Corporate Bonds: These bonds are issued by companies to raise capital for expansion or operations. Corporate bonds may offer attractive interest rates than government bonds but come with relatively higher risk.
• Convertible Bonds: These bonds can be converted into a specified number of shares of the issuing company, providing potential upside if the company’s stock performs well.
• Zero-Coupon Bonds: These bonds are sold at a discount and do not pay interest periodically. Instead, they mature at face value, with the difference representing your return.
Key Features of
Bonds
Bonds come with the following features:
• Interest Payments: Bonds provide regular income through interest payments, known as coupons. These payments are usually made either semi-annually or annually, offering you a predictable stream of income throughout the life of the bond.
• Maturity Date: This is the date when the bond reaches the end of its term, and the issuer is required to repay the principal amount to the bondholder.
• Credit Rating: Bonds are evaluated and rated based on the issuer’s creditworthiness. This rating indicates the bond’s risk level and potential returns, with higher ratings signifying lower risk and generally lower yields, while lower ratings suggest higher risk but potentially higher returns.
Advantages of
Bonds
With bond investments, you can benefit from the following:
• Predictable and Regular Income: Bonds offer a stable income stream through regular interest payments.

• Holding
In bonds, the holding can be in two forms: physical certificates or dematerialized (demat) format. Demat holding is more common, offering easy transfer, sale, and tracking. Bonds can also be traded in the secondary market, allowing flexibility in ownership.
Fixed deposits are usually held with the issuing bank. Ownership is simpler, as FDs do not involve trading. They are locked for a fixed tenure, with the investor receiving interest payouts at regular intervals or upon maturity, depending on the chosen option.

Most bank FDs are not rated by credit rating agencies since they are considered secure by virtue of being offered by regulated banks. Deposits up to ₹5 lakh are insured by the DICGC. mind. 
[Fixed
deposits](https://altifi.ai/) and bonds
are among the most popular investments providing regular returns to investors.
While the objective of the two modes may be similar, FDs and bonds have
different features that investors need to understand before deciding which one
to choose.
FDs, especially those issued by
banks, have traditionally been the most favoured fixed income instrument for
Indian households. However, the preferences as the bond [market](https://altifi.ai/) grows with more
issuances and with increasing ease of investing, especially through the comfort
of online investing, they also come up as an attractive avenue for safe and
regular income.
Here we discuss the features of both the instruments and how they compare as investment alternatives.
Difference in features
[Bonds](https://altifi.ai/) are generally issued by
governments, corporations and even municipalities to raise money. On the other
hand, fixed deposits are generally issued by banks, post offices, housing
finance companies and a few non-banking finance companies (NBFC).
There are various ways of bond
issuance. They can be auctioned, privately placed or offered to the public at
large through a public offer. A few bonds, such as RBI Floating Rate Savings
[Bonds](https://altifi.ai/), are available on tap through the year. Fixed deposits are available on
demand. Rarely does an issuing entity like a bank stop accepting fixed
deposits.
Fixed deposits can be renewed at the
time of maturity in case investors want to continue earning interest on the
invested amount. Investors can opt for an auto-renewal facility while booking a
[fixed deposit](https://altifi.ai/). However, the rate of interest offered on renewal may change
depending on the market conditions.
Fixed deposit issuances generally
have a minimum stipulated investment while there is no other restriction on the
amount of money invested.  Bondholders, however, are usually
paid the principal and [interest](https://altifi.ai/) earned at the time of maturity and the bond is
extinguished. The face value of the bond is predetermined and an investor has
to buy in multiple of one bond minimum.
Bonds signal risk quantum to investor
The issuer has to mandatorily get a
credit rating on their bond offering. The rating ensures investors get an idea
of the risk involved in investing in a particular bond. A higher [credit rating](https://altifi.ai/)

The backing of collateral
Bonds are of two types – secured and
unsecured. Secured [bonds](https://altifi.ai/) have underlying assets which are sold to pay off the
secured bondholders in case the issuer goes into liquidation. These bondholders
have a claim on assets ahead of other claimants with unsecured debt. Unsecured
bonds do not have earmarked collateral.
Fixed deposits are generally unsecured. However, bank fixed deposits up to Rs 5 lakh per depositor in each bank are insured by Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC).

bonds is generally taxable in the hands of the investor, unless stated
otherwise. For example, the interest payouts on the tax-free bonds are exempt
from income [tax](https://altifi.ai/).

known as Section 54EC bonds, can be used by individuals to save on tax on long
term capital gains booked on sale of property or assets.

title: Credit risk in Bonds: Get paid for managing it right
content:
“Successful investing is about managing risk, not avoiding it”: Benjamin Graham.
The shadow of ‘risk’ is lurking everywhere be it life or in investing. The investment landscape has a large canvas of risk starting with the extremely high-risk investments such as the unregulated world of Cryptocurrencies at one end to safe investments such as bonds guaranteed by the sovereign. Somewhere within the spectrum is equities with high-risk associated and plethora of debt instruments bonds with varying degree of risk.
Yes, you read it right. Debt instruments carry a fair degree of risk. Most fixed income investors are risk-averse and invest in debt to avoid sudden, unpleasant hits to their portfolio.
Types of risk:
An investment in a bond is typically exposed to three main types of risk - credit risk, liquidity risk and interest rate risk.
Credit risk is a crucial parameter for a bond and understanding it is beneficial for every investor wanting to invest in a range of debt instruments. Credit risk simply denotes the possibility of an issuer of a bond not paying the interest or principal or both on the due date as per the terms of the bond. In India this is very much evident in the past when some of the issuers failed to honor their commitments to the investors.
Liquidity risk is an uncertainty over being to sell the instruments when one needs money. Many bonds are thinly traded and cannot be easily sold to create liquidity.
On the other hand, interest rate risk refers to the impact of changes in the overall interest rate environment on the debt instrument. This has direct impact on the price of the instrument. As is evident in recent years, interest rates globally have witnessed a cycle of gradual lowering, followed by the current cycle of central banks across the world raising interest rates to tame the raging inflation. For investors who intend to hold their bonds till maturity, liquidity and interest rate risk have no impact.
In this article we look at how credit risk impacts debt and how you can understand it to make the most from your investments.
How credit rating helps:
Credit rating is a mechanism to help investors understand the overall risk level associated with debt offering. Debt issuers approach credit rating companies to measure this credit risk associated with each of the bonds. The bonds with the highest of safety of repayment of principal and interest, in the credit rating agency’s opinion, are AAA rated. As the credit risk goes up, the rating changes to lower levels such as AA+, AA, A, A+, BBB and so on. A debt instrument assigned ‘C’ rating carries very high risk for investors while a ‘D’ signifies imminent default.
However, it is important to note that credit rating agencies operate within fixed frameworks and this may sometimes prevent them from assessing the risk accurately. They can err on both sides – either being too generous or conservative in their opinions. This leads to opportunities to exploit the arbitrage between perceived risk and real risk.

title: Credit risk in Bonds: Get paid for managing it right
content:
However, it is important to note that credit rating agencies operate within fixed frameworks and this may sometimes prevent them from assessing the risk accurately. They can err on both sides – either being too generous or conservative in their opinions. This leads to opportunities to exploit the arbitrage between perceived risk and real risk. Many institutional lenders and investors have their own credit teams to assess the risk involved and exploit this arbitrage. Retail investors can also take advantage of this scenario by investing in bonds that have been curated by experts.
Impact of rating changes:
Credit ratings are issued for short term debt as well as long term debt of the issuer. Ratings are periodically reviewed by rating agencies with rating changes indicating altered fundamentals of the issuer. If a bond’s credit rating improves, the price of the bond in the secondary market goes up, with less risk visible and vice-versa. Investors would notice that the net asset value (NAV) of a mutual fund schemes holding bonds change when an instrument with sizable allocation undergoes a change in credit rating.
Improving returns:
Taking the right credit risk can enhance one’s portfolio returns. A relatively low credit rating means the coupon payments are higher compared to AAA rated bonds. Thus, an inverse relationship exists here: The higher the rating, the lower the returns. Take the simple case of credit risk funds. These mutual fund schemes invest a minimum of 65 percent of their corpus in bonds with credit rating less than AA+. These schemes are expected to offer better returns than schemes holding AAA rated bonds.
Savvy investors with greater risk-taking ability can implement this strategy in their personal portfolio by choosing to invest in bonds with lower rating. In times of high inflation, when the rate of real yield (nominal rate of interest minus inflation) is negative, investments in high coupon bonds can save the fixed income portfolio. However, since these bonds come with elevated risk, investors need to be careful by performing adequate diligence, relying on advisors or choosing curated securities vetted by experts.
Diversify your allocation:
At the overall portfolio level the allocation to such bonds needs to be decided. Also, once the overall allocation is decided, a smart investor should ensure that not all of it is invested with one issuer or issuers from one sector. This diversification helps in case of an adverse development and reduces concentration risk.
An eye on liquidity:
It may be difficult to find buyers of bonds with AA, A and BBB ratings in the secondary market. Hence, they enjoy low demand in the secondary market and may not always trade near fair value. Investors taking exposure to these bonds, hence, ideally prefer to hold on to them till maturity.
Secured vs unsecured:
Some investors are keen to only invest in low rated bonds only to the extent of secured offerings, while the more aggressive lot may choose to invest in unsecured ones.

It may be difficult to find buyers of bonds with AA, A and BBB ratings in the secondary market. Hence, they enjoy low demand in the secondary market and may not always trade near fair value. Investors taking exposure to these bonds, hence, ideally prefer to hold on to them till maturity.

Some investors are keen to only invest in low rated bonds only to the extent of secured offerings, while the more aggressive lot may choose to invest in unsecured ones.

title: Types of Corporate Bonds: Investor Guide
content:
Most people first hear about corporate bonds only after they’ve spent years investing elsewhere. Stocks feel exciting. Fixed deposits feel familiar. Bonds usually sit somewhere in between quiet, practical, and easy to ignore. Until you realise they’re doing a lot of work behind the scenes.
At a very basic level, a corporate bond is not complicated. A company needs money. Instead of taking a bank loan or issuing shares, it borrows directly from investors. In return, it agrees to pay interest and return the money after a fixed period.
That’s it.
Where things start to matter is how that borrowing is structured. Because not all corporate bonds behave the same way, and not all of them carry the same level of risk.
What a Corporate Bond Actually Is
When you buy a corporate bond, you are lending money to a company for a defined period.
In exchange, the company mentions:
- regular interest payments (monthly, quarterly, or annually)
- repayment of your principal on a specific maturity date
Companies use this money to expand capacity, fund projects, refinance old debt, or manage cash flows. Investors use bonds to generate income and add stability to their portfolios.
Types of Corporate Bonds Based on Security
[Corporate bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/corporate-bonds) can be categorised according to their repayment priority and the security that underpins them.
- Secured Bonds: These bonds are backed by assets of the corporation. The pledged assets may be utilised to satisfy repayment obligations in case of the issuer defaults.
- Unsecured Bonds (debentures): These bonds are not secured by any specific security. Repayment is contingent upon the issuer's financial stability and capacity to fulfil commitments.
Types of Corporate Bonds Based on Repayment Priority
Here are the types of corporate bonds based on their repayment priority.
- Senior Bonds: During repayment, these bonds have a greater claim on corporate assets. Subordinated debt holders are often paid after senior bondholders.
- Subordinated Bonds: In the system of repayment, these bonds are ranked lower than senior debt. After paying higher-priority creditors, repayment is typically made.
Types of Corporate Bonds Based on Equity Features
Some corporate bonds include provisions that are linked to company shares.
- Partly Convertible Bonds: A portion of the bond can be exchanged into equity shares of the issuing company. The remaining portion continues as a regular debt instrument until maturity.
- Mandatory Convertible Bonds: These bonds automatically convert into shares on a specified date. The conversion takes place according to conditions mentioned in the issue documents.
Types of Corporate Bonds Based on Conversion Features
Some corporate bonds have different conversion rules.
- Convertible Bonds: Under certain conditions, these bonds may be convert for equity shares. At the time of issuance, the conversion price and ratio are determined.
- Non-Convertible Bonds: These bonds are not convertible into equity shares.

The conversion takes place according to conditions mentioned in the issue documents.
Types of Corporate Bonds Based on Conversion Features
Some corporate bonds have different conversion rules.
- Convertible Bonds: Under certain conditions, these bonds may be convert for equity shares. At the time of issuance, the conversion price and ratio are determined.
- Non-Convertible Bonds: These bonds are not convertible into equity shares. According to the bond terms, investors get principal and interest payments.
Types of Corporate Bonds Based on Interest and Redemption Structure
Corporate bonds may also vary in terms of how interest is paid and how maturity is defined.
- Fixed Rate Bonds: These are bonds that pay a fixed rate of interest over the term of the bond. The coupon rate is fixed regardless of what happens to the market interest rate.
- Floating Rate Bonds: These bonds have changed interest rates. The rate is generally linked to a benchmark or reference rate.
- Zero Coupon Bonds: There are no monthly interest payments on these bonds. They sell at a discount on the face value and redeem at face value upon maturity.
- Callable Bonds: The issuer can repay these bonds before maturity.
- Puttable Bonds: These bonds give investors the option to sell them back early. The exercise conditions are defined when the bonds are issued.
- Perpetual Bonds: These are bonds that have no set maturity date. Interest payments are expected to continue as long as the issuer is liable.
Bonds Based on Maturity
Time horizon changes how a bond behaves.
- Short-term bonds (1–3 years): Lower volatility, easier exits
- Medium-term bonds (4–10 years): Balanced risk and return
- Long-term bonds (10+ years): Higher yields, but more sensitive to interest rate changes
Matching maturity to your financial goals is often more important than chasing yield.
Choosing the Right Corporate Bond
There’s no universally “best” bond. The right one depends on context.
- How much risk can you actually tolerate?
- Do you need regular income or future lump sums?
- How comfortable are you holding till maturity?
- Can you exit easily if needed?
- Good bond investing is usually about balance, not bravado.
Conclusion
Corporate bonds may serve as a suitable instrument for regular income. They may offer cash flows, defined maturity periods, and varying risk profiles depending on issuer quality and structure. Understanding bond categories, credit strength, and investment horizon helps improve decision-making and reduces exposure to unnecessary risk. A disciplined approach ensures alignment with financial goals, liquidity needs, and risk tolerance. When used appropriately, corporate bonds may contribute to portfolio stability and long-term financial planning outcomes.
FAQs
Are corporate bonds safe?
They may be relatively less volatile than equities but riskier than government bonds. It depends on the issuer and bond structure.
How much do corporate bonds pay?
Typically between 8% and 12%, depending on credit quality and maturity.

Diversification Beyond Stocks: 5 Ways Bonds Enhance Your Portfolio
An investment portfolio is a collection or a set of financial assets that an investor owns. It may include stocks, mutual funds, commodities, equities, etc. A smart investor will always maintain a diversified investment portfolio to spread their investment risk, benefit from the performance of other asset classes and tap into the earning opportunities that every investment avenue offers. Bonds are one among them. If you are an investor looking to diversify your portfolio beyond stocks, here’s how bonds can help amplify your overall portfolio strength.
What are Bonds?
A bond is a fixed-income investment. It represents a debt that involves an investor loaning money to a government or a company for a specified time. The government or company is the issuer of the bond. It agrees to repay the principal amount that the investor invests while buying the bond and pay a particular interest periodically.
Companies and governments issue bonds to raise funds for various purposes like funding projects, operational expansion, project completion, buying equipment, cash flow management, etc. Bonds are deemed to be carrying a lower risk than stocks as they pay a regular interest and repay the principal amount at maturity. However, it should be noted that bond prices can vary depending on factors like interest rate fluctuations, issuer’s credit quality, macroeconomic conditions, etc.
Type of Bonds
Let’s look at some types of bonds you may consider investing in.
- [Government Bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/government-securities): As the name suggests, these bonds are issued by the Government of India. They are considered safer to invest in, considering the government backing and guarantee they have. These bonds are issued to fund infrastructure development projects.
- [Corporate Bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/corporate-bonds): These bonds are issued by corporations to fund their projects or various financial objectives. Some types of corporate bonds include public sector undertaking (PSU) bonds or private corporate bonds.
- Convertible Bonds: As the name indicates, one can convert these bonds into a predetermined number of shares of the issuing organisation’s stock.
- Zero-Coupon Bonds: These bonds are sold at a discount to their face value and do not pay any period interest. Instead of that the investor receives the bond’s face value upon its maturity.
- Perpetual Bonds: Perpetual bonds do not have any maturity date but pay interest indefinitely. However, they allow the issuer to buy back or redeem the bond after a particular period.
Advantages of Investing in Bonds
Now, why do we say bonds can enhance your portfolio? Of course, we’ll discuss the various ways in which they do it. However, before that, let’s look at a few advantages that denote the importance of bonds in a modern-day investment portfolio.

title: Diversify & Strengthen Your Portfolio: 5 Benefits of Bond Investing
content:
Advantages of Investing in Bonds
Now, why do we say bonds can enhance your portfolio? Of course, we’ll discuss the various ways in which they do it. However, before that, let’s look at a few advantages that denote the importance of bonds in a modern-day investment portfolio.
Fixed Income Stream:
Who doesn’t want to receive regular income from a reliable source? Everyone does! Bonds offer periodic interest payments, which can serve as a fixed income stream for investors. Thus, they prove a promising investment alternative in this regard. Besides, the consistency and regularity of income generation make bonds a predictable income source for every investor looking for steady and fixed income.
Capital Preservation:
When it comes to volatility, bonds usually are considered less volatile than stocks. Hence, they are a more conservative investment choice and offer the potential for capital preservation, especially if investors hold them until maturity.
Liquidity:
Bonds are usually more liquid than other fixed-income investment avenues like saving accounts, etc. Investors can easily buy and sell them in the secondary market, thus offering investors a certain amount of flexibility.
Tax Benefits:
A few bond types, for instance, municipal bonds may offer tax advantages. Meaning, that the interest income investors earn through municipal bonds is exempt from the national tax regulations. However, investors should check the tax implications of a particular bond before they invest in it.
Diversification:
So, we finally come to diversification. Bonds can help you diversify your investment portfolio, helping an investor spread the investment risk across various asset classes. When a particular investment avenue, for example if stocks perform poorly, bonds may hold or increase in value, providing a buffer against market downwaves.
Strengthening Your Investment Portfolio – 5 Ways Bonds Can Do It
Here’s how bonds can augment your portfolio value.
Risk Mitigation:
Bonds can prove an excellent option if you are looking to diversify your portfolio. How? They are safer than mutual funds and stocks as they offer a fixed income and are less volatile. Thus, including bond investments in your portfolio can help mitigate your overall investment risk and offset any uncertainty arising from equities or other volatile investment options. Accordingly, investing in bonds can help protect your investment capital and strengthen the base of your portfolio, making it more bankable.
Predictable and Stable Income:
The investment playground caters to different types of investors. While some look to build quick wealth and sizeable profits through high-risk investments, many look at the bigger picture and invest in steady investment options like bonds. Why? As mentioned earlier, bonds involve paying a specific periodic interest to the investor. That interest income serves as a predictable and stable income for them.
Thus, if you are an investor looking to build a steady, stable and predictable source of income, you can consider investing in bonds.

title: Don't Ignore RBI Rules! How They Impact Bond Market Returns in India
content:
While making investment decisions, with a view to optimise total
gains, it is common among seasoned investors to prioritise analyses pertaining
to the corporations or firms they're planning to bank upon. Indeed, this
practice is vital and should be encouraged, but true financial wisdom lies in
not hyper focusing on this aspect alone. While it is important to track these
particulars, it is equally crucial to keep a tab on policy changes and
regulations that inform the said changes to a reasonable extent. The importance
of doing so is further underlined when the products in question are
market-linked. In India, major policy changes affiliated with macro-economic
stability are facilitated by the [Reserve Bank of India](https://altifi.ai/sections/blogs/rbi-liquidity-management-90-years-stability) (RBI).
As a [bond](https://altifi.ai/bonds) investor, how
important is it to comprehend the rules and regulations proposed by the RBI? To
what extent do they impact the bond market?
Regulatory Answers To Issues Plaguing The Indian Bond Market
Unlike how many understand this subject, the purpose of market regulations is not to hamper growth or individual returns, but to maintain market stability. Thus, the RBI’s core intention pertains to intervening positively for the greater good of the investors and the wider economy at large.
Keeping this in mind, it is worthwhile to explore the challenges
that are prevalent in the Indian [bond](https://altifi.ai/sections/blogs/what-is-a-bond) market and to know how policy changes by the RBI affect them. 
Dealing with Liquidity
In the context of every category of products that are market-linked, liquidity management never ceases to be a core concern. In accordance with the demands of the situation, the RBI steps in with a status-quoist mindset to prevent a liquidity crisis. For instance, it conducts Open Market Operations (OMO) with a view to keep bond yields in check, thereby also ensuring that bond prices are not reasonably affected. To be precise, OMO refers to the process of the RBI actively buying government bonds and securities from banks and investors to prevent a demand-supply mismatch. As a result, in simple words, an increase in buying interest with respect to bond products allows investors to realise their investments at a premium.
In the process, investors and organisations are further incentivized to favourably engage in the bond market and the yields are kept in check, thereby lowering the sovereign's cost of borrowing funds through the bond market.

market-linked. In India, major policy changes affiliated with macro-economic

what extent do they impact the bond market?

Unlike how many understand this subject, the purpose of market regulations is not to hamper growth or individual returns, but to maintain market stability. Thus, the RBI’s core intention pertains to intervening positively for the greater good of the investors and the wider economy at large.
Keeping this in mind, it is worthwhile to explore the challenges
that are prevalent in the Indian [bond](https://altifi.ai/sections/blogs/what-is-a-bond) market and to know how policy changes by the RBI affect them. 
Dealing with Liquidity
In the context of every category of products that are market-linked, liquidity management never ceases to be a core concern. In accordance with the demands of the situation, the RBI steps in with a status-quoist mindset to prevent a liquidity crisis. For instance, it conducts Open Market Operations (OMO) with a view to keep bond yields in check, thereby also ensuring that bond prices are not reasonably affected. To be precise, OMO refers to the process of the RBI actively buying government bonds and securities from banks and investors to prevent a demand-supply mismatch. As a result, in simple words, an increase in buying interest with respect to bond products allows investors to realise their investments at a premium.
In the process, investors and organisations are further incentivized to favourably engage in the bond market and the yields are kept in check, thereby lowering the sovereign's cost of borrowing funds through the bond market.
