In the process, investors and organisations are further incentivized to favourably engage in the bond market and the yields are kept in check, thereby lowering the sovereign's cost of borrowing funds through the bond market.
Managing Interest Rates
The state of debt supply, policy changes in the international arena, fluctuations in the indexes of influential asset classes and changes in prices of oil - both individually and in confluence with other changes - impact bond interest rates, thereby increasing the cost of borrowing funds for the government and for corporations. To ameliorate this situation, the RBI intervenes through a number of policy changes, including adjusting the repo rate - the interest rate at which banks borrow funds from RBI.
For instance, in a rising interest rate environment, a decreased repo rate allows the interest rates to get lowered, thereby keeping bond yields from rising above and bond prices from falling below the ideal range.
Besides this, the RBI also allows banks to avoid Market-To-Market Provisioning (MTM), wherein banks are obligated to record gains and losses pertaining to changes in bond prices even before realising the same, through the influx of Held-To-Maturity (HTM) bonds. The latter allows the bank to take into account the original purchase prices of the concerned bonds, as opposed to the current market prices, thereby limiting the uncertainty associated with dealing in bonds.
Enabling Market Access
While the bond market has grown tremendously over the last 3 decades, the larger share of investors remain insulated from access to these markets for several reasons. In the recent past, the RBI has attempted to enhance the situation by introducing the Retail Direct Scheme, to encourage direct investment in bond markets. While it is known that investors deal in bonds indirectly through mutual fund managers, insurance-based investments and the like, the said move was aimed at publicizing the possibility of directly investing in bonds.
Conclusion
Having said all of the above, it is also important to admit that, despite genuine attempts, regulatory gaps persist.
For instance, the access to [corporate bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/corporate-bonds) are open to investment overwhelmingly only for select firms and
organizations. Thus, the said market remains untapped for want of easy access.
However, since these are essentially not government firms, opening up access to
the same would require a much more robust infrastructure to scrutinize the credit worthiness of the private
corporations in question. Thus, while the move is attached to the possibility
of growth, it is also prone to several risks and challenges - precisely why the
regulatory gap prevails.

title: Don't Let Taxes Eat Your Bond Gains: A Smart Investor's Guide
content:
Tax Considerations for Bond Investors
Considerable portions of our discussions on investments consist of
debates on interest rates, long term growth, sustainability and the like.
However, more often than not and especially in the case of non-seasoned
investors, it’s only when our accountant charts out our tax obligations for the
year that we realise that we had probably erred in not appropriately
considering the tax implications of our investment decisions. Since factoring
in this component can significantly alter the net returns we gain from our
investments, our choice to ignore its specificities during the decision-making
process is unwise at best and blunderous at worst. While it is not uncommon for
investors to delegate this task to their financial advisors, as a matter of
principle, it is always ideal to keep a tab on our investment decisions
ourselves. As a bond investor, how does the prevalent tax regime impact your
gains on [bond investments](https://altifi.ai/sign_up)?
Taxable Income Components
In India, in respect of bond investments, there are two income components that are taxable – the income derived from interest payments and the income derived through capital gains.
In the case of the former, the interest income is added to your total income and the resultant income is then taxed in accordance with your income tax slab rate.
On the other hand, the income derived from capital gains is taxed subjectively as per the tax rules concerning Short Term Capital Gains (STCG) and Long Term Capital Gains (LTCG). Moreover, the said income is taxed depending on the specific category that your bond product falls in. As far as taxation is concerned, it is useful to broadly categorise bonds into the following two types:
- Listed Bonds – If gains made through listed bonds are held for more than one year, as per the LTCG tax rules, your income is taxed at the rate of 10%. If the same are held for less than a year, then the derived income is taxed as per your income tax slab rate, in accordance with the STCG rules.
- Unlisted Bonds – With regards to unlisted bonds, if you hold your capital gains on bond investments for less than three years, the income earned through these gains is taxed as per the STCG rules and the said income is, thus, taxed as per your income tax slab rate. However, if you decide to hold your gains for more than three years, then the concerned income is considered as part of the LTCG bracket and is taxed at the rate of 20%.
It is pertinent here to note that the indexation benefit, which factors in the inflation level while enhancing the value of your assets, is not considered while evaluating your tax obligations with respect to gains made through bond investments.

While the above-mentioned framework is applicable to Regular Taxable Bonds, there exist other types of bond products which are linked with differing tax rules within the same framework.

retirement stage or are in a situation where they ideally require the influx of
stable regular income. 
Besides these, the market also offers investors the choice of investing in Tax-Saving Bonds. content:
The economy has a big effect on the financial markets where
they work. Both stocks and corporate bonds are basic financial tools that are
very sensitive to changes in the economy as a whole. Investors who want to make
smart choices and lower their risk need to know how these things work. This
article talks about how important economic indicators affect the values of
stocks and corporate bonds, how global and domestic factors work together, and
how to use this information to make the best investments.
Important Economic Indicators That Move Financial Markets
Economic indicators tell investors where the economy is going and how healthy
it is. Some important metrics are:Gross Domestic Product (GDP) 1. GDP growth
shows how well the economy is doing as a whole. A rising GDP usually means that
businesses are making more money, people are spending more money, and investors
are more confident. Strong GDP growth is good for stocks, but corporate bond
yields may stay the same or go down if the economy makes credit risk seem
lower.
2. Rates of Inflation
Inflation lowers the value of money and has an effect on interest rates. When
inflation goes up, central banks like the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) generally
raise policy rates. This might make bond prices go down because of the inverse
price-yield connection. If inflation lowers company margins or consumer demand,
stocks might also be affected.
3. Rates of Interest
Interest rates are quite important for both the stock and bond markets.
Businesses have to pay more to borrow money when interest rates go up. This
could affect profits and stock prices. When interest rates go up, though,
corporate bond values usually go down because new bonds with larger yields are
more appealing.
4. Spending and confidence of consumers
Companies make more money when people spend money, which raises stock values.
On the other hand, when people lose faith in the economy, they may buy less
goods and services, which can hurt both company profits and stock market
values.
5. Earnings of the Company
Stock prices are directly affected by how well a company does. When a company
publishes strong earnings, its stock price usually goes up. When it misses
earnings, its stock price can drop sharply. Investors might look at earnings in
relation to the state of the economy as a whole to get a full picture.

Changes in interest rates, liquidity injections, and credit easing by central

government spending on infrastructure, tax reforms, and subsidies all have an
effect on economic activity and investment returns.

Changes in interest rates, liquidity injections, and credit easing by central
banks have direct implications on financial markets. In the same way,
government spending on infrastructure, tax reforms, and subsidies all have an
effect on economic activity and investment returns.
Effect on Stock Prices
Equity markets look ahead and are quite sensitive to economic indicators:
• Positive GDP Growth: This signals that businesses
are making money, which makes people want to invest in stocks.
• Good Interest Rates: Lower borrowing costs can lead
to growth and higher stock prices.
• More money spent by consumers: This helps
industries like FMCG, autos, and consumer durables.
• Corporate Earnings: Strong earnings make investors
more confident, while bad reports might make stocks go down.
• Announcements on policy: The RBI loosening its
policies or the government giving money to businesses might boost market
sentiment.
Financial news, RBI reports, and tools like [Altifi.ai](https://altifi.ai/sections/blogs) can help
investors keep an eye on these indications to see how the market is moving and
make smart judgments about when to buy stocks.
Effect on the Prices of Corporate Bonds
Corporate bonds are debt securities whose value is determined by both
issuer-specific and macroeconomic factors:
1. Interest Rate Sensitivity: The prices of corporate
bonds go down when interest rates go up. When rates go up, bond prices go down.
When rates go down, existing bonds become more valuable.
2. Credit Ratings: Issuers with high ratings (AAA or
AA) usually have lower yields but more security. To get investors to buy bonds
with bad ratings, they need to offer greater rates. Find out more about [corporate bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/corporate-bonds)
issued by companies.
3. Inflation Pressure: Inflation lowers actual
returns, which makes investors want higher rates to make up for it.
4. Economic Outlook: When things are uncertain or in
a recession, investors may prefer safer bonds, which raises their prices.
5. The dynamics of supply and demand in the market:
The size of the issuance, liquidity, and activity in the secondary market can
all affect bond prices. Investors may easily keep an eye on these developments
with platforms like [Altifi.ai](https://altifi.ai/bonds).
How the Global Economy Affects Local Markets

title: Factors Affecting Bond Yields in India | RBI Policy, Inflation & Market Trends
content:
Introduction
Yield-to-Maturity (YTM) represents the annualized return an investor would earn if a bond is purchased at its current market price and held until maturity, assuming all coupon payments and principal are received as scheduled. YTM considers the bond’s coupon payments and the redemption value at maturity, offering a comprehensive measure of return. When a bond is purchased, the prevailing yield indicates the expected return if held to maturity. If interest rates decrease after the bond is purchased, its market value generally rises due to the inverse relationship between bond prices and yields. Conversely, if interest rates rise, the bond's market value may fall, although the original yield is preserved (in fixed coupon bonds) if the bond is held to maturity and the issuer meets all obligations.
Economic Factors and Central Bank Actions
Bond yields are influenced by a range of macroeconomic indicators, including inflation, GDP growth, and monetary policy expectations. A key driver of interest rate decisions in India is the policy stance of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which is communicated through adjustments to the repo rate. As of August 2025, the repo rate stands at 5.50%.
Historically, when inflation is elevated, the RBI may consider increasing interest rates to maintain price stability. Conversely, in periods of lower economic growth, rate reductions may be used to support expansion. These decisions are influenced by various data points including food prices, rainfall patterns, and industrial output.
According to the RBI’s Monetary Policy Statement (August 2025), the GDP growth rate for 2024–25 was estimated at 6.5%, and the same growth rate is projected for 2025–26. This projection suggests a balanced policy stance with no immediate indication of further rate changes, subject to evolving economic conditions.
Demand-Supply Dynamics
Bond yields are also shaped by the interplay of bond issuance and investor demand. The supply side includes issuances from both government and corporate entities. Higher fiscal deficits or increased capital expenditure by corporates typically lead to greater bond issuance.
As per the Union Budget 2025–26, the fiscal deficit target is set at 4.4% of GDP. A declining deficit may reduce the volume of government borrowing, which can exert downward pressure on yields, all else being equal.
Transmission Mechanisms
Changes in the RBI’s policy rate influence the bond market through two primary channels. First, market participants often adjust their expectations and prices in anticipation of monetary policy moves. Second, actual changes in the repo rate impact short-term money market rates, which subsequently affect medium- and long-term bond yields.
Global monetary policy trends may also influence domestic bond yields.

title: How to Build a Healthy Bond Portfolio: Key Factors
content:
Bonds are fixed-income instruments that can play an important role in portfolio construction by offering income potential, diversification, and exposure to different risk-return profiles. Investors may consider bonds for various financial goals, including capital preservation, regular income generation, or balancing exposure to other asset classes. Since bonds are available in different forms, such as government bonds, corporate bonds, tax-free bonds, and inflation-linked bonds, building a healthy bond portfolio requires careful consideration of factors such as investment goals, risk tolerance, credit quality, liquidity needs, and investment horizon.
Why Does a Balanced Bond Portfolio Matters?
A bond portfolio that includes different types of bonds can help investors manage various risks associated with fixed-income investing. Since different bond categories react differently to interest-rate changes, credit conditions, and economic developments, diversification within a bond portfolio may support a more balanced investment approach.
Rather than allocating investments equally across bond types, investors typically select bonds based on their financial goals, investment horizon, income requirements, and risk tolerance.
A balanced bond portfolio may offer the following benefits:
Diversification Across Issuers: Holding bonds issued by governments, public sector entities, and corporations may reduce concentration in a single issuer or sector.
Exposure to Different Maturity Periods: Including short-, medium-, and long-term bonds may help spread investments across various time horizons and manage reinvestment considerations.
Varied Risk and Return Characteristics: Different bond categories have distinct credit profiles and income potential. Combining multiple bond types may provide exposure to a broader range of fixed-income investments.
Alignment With Financial Goals: Investors may select bonds based on specific objectives such as retirement planning, education funding, capital preservation, or regular income requirements.
Flexibility Across Market Conditions: Since bond segments may respond differently to economic and market developments, diversification may help reduce dependence on a single market outcome.
Types of Bonds You Can Invest In
Understanding the characteristics of different bond categories may help investors determine how each may fit within an overall fixed-income strategy.
Government Bonds: Issued by central governments to raise funds for public spending and financing needs. These bonds may offer fixed-income exposure with relatively lower credit risk.
Corporate Bonds: Issued by companies to fund business activities, expansion plans, or refinancing requirements. Their risk and return characteristics vary based on the issuer's financial position and credit profile.
Municipal Bonds: Issued by local government bodies and civic authorities to finance infrastructure and public development projects such as roads, transportation systems, and utilities.
Tax-Free Bonds: Typically issued by government-backed organisations or infrastructure entities. Depending on prevailing tax regulations, the interest earned may qualify for certain tax-related benefits.
Perpetual Bonds: Bonds that do not have a fixed maturity date. They generally provide periodic interest payments while remaining outstanding unless redeemed according to the issuer's terms.

title: How to Build a Healthy Bond Portfolio: Key Factors
content:
Tax-Free Bonds: Typically issued by government-backed organisations or infrastructure entities. Depending on prevailing tax regulations, the interest earned may qualify for certain tax-related benefits.
Perpetual Bonds: Bonds that do not have a fixed maturity date. They generally provide periodic interest payments while remaining outstanding unless redeemed according to the issuer's terms.
Inflation-Linked Bonds: Designed to adjust certain payments or principal values in line with inflation measures, potentially helping investors maintain the real value of their investments.
Specialised Bonds: These include instruments such as infrastructure bonds and sovereign gold-linked bonds, which are structured to serve specific investment objectives and policy initiatives.
The mix of bonds within a portfolio typically depends on factors such as investment goals, risk tolerance, liquidity requirements, and investment horizon.
Choosing the Right Offerings:
After figuring out how much to allocate to fixed income, investors should focus on building a mix of such instruments and decide on the quantum for each. While traditional options such as public provident fund (PPF) gives healthy tax-free returns with little credit risk, the maximum amount of money one can contribute is Rs 1.5 lakh each year. Bank fixed deposits and debt funds can also offer much-needed stability and interim liquidity to the investor. However, bonds such as non-convertible debentures and high-yield bonds play an important role when it comes to sprucing up portfolio returns since they have the potential to provide higher returns. While investing in such offerings, one should figure out details such as credit rating, rate of interest and tenure of the instrument.
The lower the rating, the higher will be the risk and consequently the returns. Bonds with credit ratings below BBB indicate high credit risk. Such bonds are meant only for aggressive fixed income investors. Most investors aiming for a relatively higher return invest in AA and A-rated bonds issued by reputed companies. Depending on the investor’s risk profile and cash-flow needs, 10-25% of the portfolio can be invested in the high-yield bonds.
Investors should spread their portfolio of bonds across companies operating in different sectors. Such diversification may reduce the risk at the portfolio level. For example, one may choose not to invest more than 5% of a bond portfolio in NCDs with AA rating issued by a gold loan company, and overall exposure to gold loan companies’ bonds may be capped at 15%.
Monitoring the Portfolio Regularly
Building a bond portfolio is not a static endeavour but rather an ongoing process that necessitates vigilance and adaptability. As financial circumstances evolve and market dynamics shift, investors must remain proactive in managing their portfolios to ensure alignment with their changing goals and risk profiles. As one ages, the risk-taking ability generally goes down. Accordingly, the asset allocation needs to be changed to safer assets such as bonds.

title: How to Build a Healthy Bond Portfolio: Key Factors
content:
Building a bond portfolio is not a static endeavour but rather an ongoing process that necessitates vigilance and adaptability. As financial circumstances evolve and market dynamics shift, investors must remain proactive in managing their portfolios to ensure alignment with their changing goals and risk profiles. As one ages, the risk-taking ability generally goes down. Accordingly, the asset allocation needs to be changed to safer assets such as bonds. Moreover, monitoring bond portfolios entails tracking interest receipts and maturity proceeds, ensuring timely reinvestment of funds to capitalise on prevailing market conditions. Idle cash reserves represent missed opportunities for growth, underscoring the importance of proactive portfolio management.
By adopting a disciplined approach to portfolio monitoring and management, investors may navigate the complexities of the bond market. Each adjustment and refinement may help in wealth accumulation and financial security.
Building a Bond Portfolio: Step by Step
Creating a bond portfolio involves selecting investments that align with your financial objectives, risk appetite, liquidity needs, and investment horizon. Since different bonds have different characteristics, investors may consider a combination of factors before deciding how to allocate their funds.
Step 1: Identify the Purpose of Your Investment
Start by defining why you want to invest in bonds. Some investors may prioritise regular income, while others may focus on capital preservation, portfolio diversification, or funding future financial goals. Your objective can influence the types of bonds and maturities you choose.
Step 2: Choose an Appropriate Mix of Bond Categories
Bonds are available in various forms, including government bonds, corporate bonds, municipal bonds, and tax-free bonds. Each category has distinct features, risks, and return characteristics. Allocating investments across different bond types may help create a more diversified fixed-income portfolio.
Step 3: Consider Maturity Distribution
Bond maturity refers to the period after which the principal amount is scheduled to be repaid. Short-term, medium-term, and long-term bonds may react differently to market conditions and interest-rate changes. Including bonds with varying maturities can help distribute investments across different time horizons.
Step 4: Evaluate Credit Quality
The financial strength of a bond issuer is an important consideration when selecting bonds. Credit ratings provide an indication of an issuer's ability to meet its repayment obligations. Investors often review credit quality alongside other factors such as investment goals and risk tolerance before making investment decisions.
Step 5: Assess Liquidity Requirements
Some bonds may be easier to sell in the secondary market than others. Investors who anticipate the need to access funds before maturity may consider liquidity as part of their bond selection process.
Step 6: Review and Rebalance Periodically
Over time, changes in interest rates, market conditions, and personal financial circumstances may affect the composition of a bond portfolio. Periodic reviews may help investors assess whether their existing allocation continues to align with their investment objectives.

Investors are increasingly embracing corporate bonds as an alternative to traditional fixed-income instruments such as FDs, PPF and postal saving schemes. The preference can be attributed to higher yield, liquidity benefits and risk-adjusted returns offered by corporate bonds.
Yield advantage
Corporate bonds offer significantly higher yields compared with traditional instruments. The yield differential can substantially impact long-term wealth creation, particularly for retirement planning.
Liquidity benefits
Corporate bonds traded on exchanges offer higher liquidity compared with PPF and postal saving schemes, which have lock-in periods ranging from five to 15 years. Thus, investors in corporate bonds can exit positions if their financial needs change or they wish to rebalance portfolios in response to interest rate movements.
Risk-adjusted returns
While corporate bonds carry an element of credit risk
compared with government-backed PPF and postal saving schemes, it is
compensated by higher yields. Investors can mitigate the risk by selecting
bonds from established companies with strong credit ratings.

title: What Are Floating-Rate Bonds? Working & Investor Benefits
content:
In an era of fluctuating interest rates, floating-rate bonds have emerged as an attractive investment avenue for investors seeking both flexibility and stable returns. Unlike traditional fixed-rate bonds, floating-rate bonds adjust their interest payouts periodically, helping investors capitalise on interest rate changes while protecting their capital from rate volatility.
In this guide, we explore the definition, features, benefits, and strategies for investing in floating-rate bonds in India, along with real-life examples.
Key Takeaways
- Floating-rate bonds have variable interest rates linked to benchmark rates, which reset periodically.
- They offer protection against rising interest rates, as coupon payments increase when benchmark rates rise.
- Prices of floating-rate bonds remain more stable than fixed-rate bonds since interest payments adjust with market rates.
- Benefits include interest rate hedging, low price volatility, portfolio diversification, and potential for higher returns.
- Investors can optimise returns by analysing yield curves, actively managing portfolios, and diversifying across issuers.
What are Floating-Rate Bonds?
Floating-rate bonds (FRBs) are debt instruments whose coupon rates are linked to a benchmark interest rate, such as the repo rate, reverse repo rate, or T-bill rates in India, or globally, the LIBOR or Federal Funds Rate.
Whenever the benchmark rate changes, the bond’s coupon payments adjust according to a predefined formula. Issuers of floating-rate bonds include governments, banks, and large corporations, with interest payments typically made quarterly, semi-annually, or annually.
Think of it like a floating-rate home loan: as the repo rate rises, the EMIs increase. Similarly, investors in FRBs receive higher interest payments when benchmark rates rise, providing a hedge against inflation and interest rate risk.
How Do Floating Rate Bonds Work?
Floating-rate bonds make interest payments at regular intervals and repay the principal amount at maturity. However, the interest rate is not fixed. It increases or decreases based on changes in the linked benchmark rate. These changes are passed on to the bond’s coupon rate on pre-set dates.
For example, consider a floating-rate bond with a face value of ₹1,00,000 that is linked to a benchmark rate, such as the central bank policy rate, with a spread of 1.5%. Assume that the bond pays interest every six months and resets its rate at the beginning of each period.
At the time of issuance, if the benchmark rate is 6%, the coupon rate for the first six months would be 7.5% (6% + 1.5%). The investor would therefore receive interest based on this rate for that period.
At the next reset date, suppose the benchmark rate rises to 7%. The coupon rate for the following six months would adjust to 8.5%. As a result, the interest payment for that period would be higher.

The investor would therefore receive interest based on this rate for that period.
At the next reset date, suppose the benchmark rate rises to 7%. The coupon rate for the following six months would adjust to 8.5%. As a result, the interest payment for that period would be higher. Since the rate is reset periodically, it tends to stay aligned with prevailing market rates. This structure helps reduce interest rate risk, especially during periods of rising interest rates.

Mechanics of Floating-Rate Bonds
Floating-rate bonds have three key components:
1. Coupon Rate:
The interest rate on FRBs is tied to a benchmark rate plus a fixed spread. In India, it could be linked to NSC, repo rate, or T-bills, while globally it may track LIBOR or US Treasury rates.
2. Coupon Reset:
Interest rates are periodically reset (quarterly or semi-annually) based on market benchmarks, allowing investors to capture rate changes over time.
3. Interest Payments:
Payments are calculated by applying the reset coupon rate to the bond’s principal. For example, a bond with a principal of INR 100,000 and a 7% floating coupon will pay INR 3,500 semi-annually if the rate is 7%.
Example: RBI Floating-Rate Bond
The RBI’s floating-rate bonds are linked to the National Savings Certificate (NSC) rate plus 0.35% spread. Suppose an individual invest INR 100,000 in July 2020 with semi-annual interest payments.
- Jan–Jun 2023: NSC rate change results in INR 3,675 per 6 months
- Jul–Dec 2023: Coupon rises to INR 4,025 per 6 months
This example shows how interest payments fluctuate in sync with benchmark rates, providing an effective hedge against interest rate changes.
Taxation of RBI Floating Rate Bonds
Taxation is an important aspect to consider before investing in these bonds:
- Interest income is taxed as per the investor’s income tax slab
- Capital gains for a holding period of less than one year are taxed as per slab rates
- Capital gains for a holding period above one year are taxed at 12.5% without indexation
Benefits of Investing in Floating-Rate Bonds
Hedge Against Rising Rates:
FRBs adjust with market rates, protecting investors from the adverse effects of interest rate hikes.
Low Price Volatility:
Since coupon rates reset periodically, FRBs maintain stable market prices compared to fixed-rate bonds.
Credit Safety:
Issued by governments and high-creditworthy institutions, FRBs generally carry low default risk.
Potential for Higher Returns:
Investors benefit when interest rates trend upward, capturing better yields than fixed-rate bonds.
Portfolio Diversification:
FRBs provide an alternative fixed-income asset, balancing equity and fixed deposits in a diversified portfolio.

Limitations of Floating Rate Bonds
The limitations of investing in floating-rate bonds are as follows:
- Lower Yield: Floating-rate bonds may offer lower overall returns compared to fixed-rate bonds.
- Uncertainty of Income: The interest income is not constant and may vary over time due to periodic changes in the benchmark rate.
- Interest Rate Risk: Since the coupon rate is not fixed, returns may decrease when interest rates fall. This can lead to lower income compared to fixed-rate bonds.
Factors Affecting the RBI Floating Bonds Interest Rate
Factors that can affect the interest rate of RBI floating rate bonds include:
- Inflation Trends: Changes in inflation affect the benchmark interest rate in the economy. When inflation rises, benchmark rates increase, leading to higher interest rates on bonds. However, benchmark rates decrease when inflation reduces. So, the bond’s interest rate also decrease.
- Economic Trends: Economic trends can play a major role in the change in interest rates and benchmarks linked to these bonds.
- Repo Rate Changes: The repo rate set by the RBI can play a major part in determining the interest rates. Hence indirectly affecting the interest rates of floating-rate bonds.
How to Invest?
Investing in floating-rate bonds generally involves the following steps:
- Select a suitable platform, like a nationalised bank, private bank, or the RBI Retail Direct platform
- Access the bond investment section
- Fill in the required details and select the investment amount
- Submit the necessary documents, such as PAN and address proof
- Complete the application process
- Once processed, the interest is usually credited directly to the registered bank account.
Documents Required
To invest in floating-rate bonds, certain documents are generally required:
- Completed application form with personal details
- Cancelled cheque
- Investment amount details
- Self-attested PAN card
- Self-attested address proof
Strategies to Capitalise on Interest Rate Movements
- Yield Curve Analysis: Position investments along the yield curve to anticipate rate changes.
- Active Portfolio Management: Regularly review allocations to maximise returns while managing risk.
- Diversification: Spread investments across sectors, issuers, and tenures to mitigate credit and rate risks.
Conclusion
Floating-rate bonds are a powerful tool for investors seeking interest rate protection and flexible returns. By actively managing allocations and monitoring benchmark rates, investors can hedge against inflation and rising interest rates while maintaining a diversified, low-risk portfolio.

title: Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs) Explained
content:
Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs) function as hybrid securities which have characteristics of both debt and equity. Investors receive the bonds which are designated in foreign currencies, and they can convert them to shares at a predetermined price which will be valid until a future date. FCCBs function like standard bonds because they provide investors with predetermined interest payments which continue until the bonds reach their designated end date. The conversion option benefits investors when the company's stock value increases. The companies generally use FCCBs to obtain funds from global markets at reduced expenses.
How Do FCCBs Work?
FCCBs involve a process in which both benefits of borrowing and investing are equally addressed. When a company issues FCCBs, it raises capital in a foreign currency from overseas investors. These bonds are offered at a coupon rate, which is relatively lower than other debt instruments.
Every FCCB has a conversion price that is the price at which the bond can be converted into equity shares. If the price of the company’s shares increases beyond the conversion price, the investors can convert the bond into shares and enjoy the benefits of price appreciation.
If the share price is not doing well, the investors can opt to hold the bond until maturity and receive the principal amount along with interest payments.
FCCBs may also include:
- Call options, allowing the issuer to redeem the bond before maturity
- Put options, allowing investors to exit early under certain conditions
At maturity, one of three outcomes usually takes place:
- Conversion into equity shares
- Redemption in foreign currency
- Partial conversion with balance repayment
Overall, FCCBs offer flexibility. They work well in situations where companies want access to global funds while giving investors multiple exit options.
Key Features of Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds
Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs) have special characteristics, which distinguish them from other bonds and equity products. These special characteristics make FCCBs a popular and accepted funding option for many companies across the globe.
- Issued in Foreign Currencies: These bonds are issued in a currency such as USD or EUR rather than the company's local currency. This exposes the company and investors to currency risk.
- Lower Coupon Rate: The rate of return on FCCBs is relatively low compared to regular bonds issued in the domestic market. This is because the investor receives an additional benefit in the form of an equity conversion option.
- Equity Conversion Option: This is an important characteristic of FCCBs that differentiates them from regular bonds and debt instruments. The bondholders have the option to convert the bond into equity shares at a predetermined price.
- Fixed Maturity Period: FCCBs have a fixed maturity date. After the maturity date, the bonds can be converted into equity, or the company can redeem the bonds.
- Hybrid Instrument: FCCBs combine the stability of debt and the growth opportunities of equity instruments. This potentially makes FCCBs suitable to a wide range of investors.

- Hybrid Instrument: FCCBs combine the stability of debt and the growth opportunities of equity instruments. This potentially makes FCCBs suitable to a wide range of investors.
- Access to International Investors: These bonds provide companies with an opportunity to raise funds from global markets. This helps companies access a wider investor base.
Advantages and Disadvantages of FCCBs
Here are some advantages and disadvantages of Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds:
| Category | For Companies | For Investors | 
| Advantages | Lower borrowing cost due to conversion option | Downside protection through fixed interest income | 
| | Access to global capital markets | Potential equity upside if share price rises | 
| | Deferred equity dilution until conversion | Portfolio diversification with foreign currency exposure | 
| | Possible tax benefits on interest payments | Balanced risk-return structure | 
| Disadvantages / Risks | Exchange rate risk due to foreign currency borrowing | Credit risk if issuer faces financial issues | 
| | Equity dilution if bonds are converted | Liquidity risk in secondary markets | 
| | Redemption pressure if conversion does not happen | Uncertain gains if the stock underperforms | 
RBI Regulatory Framework for FCCBs
In India, FCCBs are governed under the broader framework of External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs), regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
Key regulatory requirements include:
- Minimum Maturity Period: The FCCBs must have at least five years of maturity time because their primary function is to support funding needs that extend beyond this duration.
- Annual Borrowing Limit: The automatic route permits companies to obtain up to USD 750 million, while any greater amount requires special permission from the Reserve Bank of India.
- End-use Restrictions: The funds can be raised for capital expenditure and investment abroad, but not for real estate and stock market investment.
- Cost Ceiling: The total cost of funds is subject to RBI guidelines, including interest and other associated costs.
- Eligible Issuers: Only companies that qualify under the RBI's financial and regulatory requirements are allowed to raise FCCBs.
- Reporting requirements: All transactions must be reported to the RBI through authorised banks using prescribed forms.
Tax Implications for FCCB Investors
The tax responsibility for Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds in India requires multiple procedures which depend on whether an investor maintains bond ownership or receives interest payments or transforms the bond into stock.
- Interest Income: Investors from non-resident countries must pay 10% Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) for any interest they receive on FCCBs because Section 194LC of the Income Tax Act 1961 mandates this requirement.

content:
- Interest Income: Investors from non-resident countries must pay 10% Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) for any interest they receive on FCCBs because Section 194LC of the Income Tax Act 1961 mandates this requirement. This condition only applies to bonds which were issued before the date specified in the Finance Act.
- Conversion of Debt to Equity: An FCCB conversion to equity shares creates no tax obligation according to Section 47 of the Income Tax Act. This means that no capital gains tax will be applied to this type of conversion.
- Selling Converted Shares: Once converted to an equity share, any sale of such shares will attract normal capital gains tax. The cost of acquisition will be taken as the face value of the bond at the time of conversion.
- Redemption of Debt Without Conversion: When an investor does not convert an FCCB to an equity share, any excess amount received at maturity over and above the initial investment will attract income tax.
- DTAA benefits: Non-resident investors may benefit from lower withholding tax rates if a Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) exists between India and their country of residence.
Disclaimer: Tax rules for FCCBs are subject to change based on amendments to the Finance Act, RBI circulars, and DTAA provisions. Investors should consult a qualified tax adviser before making investment decisions. TDS applicable as per IT rules. Interest rates are subject to change.
Famous Examples of FCCBs in India
Several Indian companies have used foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCBs) to raise capital, with mixed outcomes.
Tata Motors (2009–2014)
Tata Motors raised around USD 750 million through FCCBs. As its share price rose over time, many investors converted their bonds into equity, making it a successful case for both the company and investors.
Suzlon Energy
Suzlon Energy issued FCCBs worth over USD 500 million, but its share price declined. Most investors did not convert, leading to a large repayment burden and debt restructuring.
These examples show that FCCB outcomes largely depend on share price performance and exchange rate movements at maturity.

Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs) serve as an effective method for organisations to gather funds and allocate those funds. Several Indian companies have used foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCBs) to raise capital, with mixed outcomes.

Suzlon Energy issued FCCBs worth over USD 500 million, but its share price declined. Most investors did not convert, leading to a large repayment burden and debt restructuring.

The securities provide investors with bond-like fixed income payments while granting them the right to take part in company stock value increases. However, it enables businesses to obtain international funds at reduced expenses, while it delivers secure investment growth opportunities to investors. FCCBs maintain their status as a dependable funding solution which operates effectively within today’s dynamic financial environment.

Corporates issue FCCBs to raise funds from global markets at relatively lower rates of interest. They also enjoy the advantage of delayed equity dilution along with a wider band of global investors.

title: How Geopolitical Events Influence Global Bond Markets | Bond Yield Trends
content:
Introduction
Movements in global bond markets are typically observed through changes in yields, particularly those of government securities. The yield on a 10-year government bond often serves as a key benchmark. Yield fluctuations are influenced by a range of factors including inflation, fiscal deficits, monetary policy, and supply-demand dynamics in bond markets.
Geopolitical developments, while less predictable and more situational in nature, have historically demonstrated the potential to influence bond yields. These impacts, however, vary across regions and contexts.
Historical Context - Systemic Crises and Yield Movements
The global financial crisis of 2008, though not a geopolitical event, provides context for understanding bond market responses to systemic uncertainty. In response to severe market dislocations, the US Federal Reserve lowered the federal funds rate to a range of 0% to 0.25% and injected substantial liquidity into the system. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury fell from approximately 4.3% in mid-2008 to around 2.2% by year-end.
The Russia–Ukraine Conflict
The onset of conflict between Russia and Ukraine in February 2022 led to significant policy responses. The Central Bank of Russia increased its key policy rate from 9.5% to 20% on 28 February 2022 in an effort to stabilise financial markets. Over subsequent months, the policy rate was gradually reduced to 7.5% by September 2022. The central bank later resumed rate hikes, reaching 18% by August 2025.
Such shifts illustrate how geopolitical tensions can lead to sharp policy adjustments, often with varied effects on domestic bond markets.
Regional Tensions and Global Market Reactions
Tensions involving Israel and non-state actors such as Hamas have not resulted in major dislocations in global bond markets. According to market commentary and regional analysis, limited sovereign-to-sovereign engagement and contained geographic escalation have reduced the scale of broader economic impacts. However, potential risks remain if conflicts were to affect crude oil supply chains significantly.
Yield Movements Amid US Policy and Political Developments
Between September and December 2024, the US Federal Reserve reduced the target rate by 100 basis points. Despite this, the 10-year US Treasury yield rose from 3.62% to 4.74% by 10 January 2025. Market analysts have attributed this movement to various factors, including fiscal policy expectations, foreign capital flows, and currency dynamics. These factors reflect the complex interactions between monetary policy, investor sentiment, and political developments.
Domestic Context - India’s Bond Market Environment
India’s domestic bond market has remained relatively stable during recent geopolitical shifts.

Domestic Context - India’s Bond Market Environment
India’s domestic bond market has remained relatively stable during recent geopolitical shifts. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) considers global factors such as US Federal Reserve policy actions and the USD-INR exchange rate when formulating monetary policy. However, primary emphasis remains on domestic inflation and growth trends.
Global developments such as elevated crude oil prices or slowing global GDP growth can affect India indirectly. Higher crude prices tend to raise domestic inflation, while weaker global demand may moderate export-driven growth. Despite these linkages, India’s large domestic economy provides a degree of insulation from external shocks.
Conclusion
Geopolitical uncertainty has, in past instances, influenced monetary policy responses and market sentiment, which in turn have affected bond yields across regions. These effects, however, are context-dependent and typically interwoven with broader economic factors.

content:
Gold Bonds vs Gold ETFs
Gold has long been recognized as a hedge against economic uncertainty. In 2025, global inflation, geopolitical tensions, and volatile equity markets have reinforced gold’s appeal as a safe-haven asset. Total global gold investment demand reached a record 4,974 tonnes, valued at $382 billion, signaling a renewed interest in gold-backed instruments.
Investors in India have multiple avenues to gain exposure to
gold, primarily through Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) and Gold ETFs. Understanding
their features, tax implications, and liquidity is essential for making
informed investment decisions. Platforms like [Altifi.ai](https://altifi.ai) provide a seamless way to explore and invest in
these gold instruments.
Key Takeaways
- Global demand for gold investment increased 25% in 2024, highlighting its role as a safe asset.
- SGBs pay a fixed interest of 2.5% per year in addition to potential capital gains from gold price appreciation.
- Gold ETFs offer liquidity, allowing investors to buy and sell on stock exchanges during market hours.
- Long-term SGB investors (8 years) enjoy tax-exempt capital gains, while ETFs incur taxes even for long-term holdings.
- SGBs are backed by the Reserve Bank of India, providing safety, whereas ETFs are suited for active investors seeking flexibility.
Comparing SGBs and Gold ETFs
| Basis | Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) | Gold ETFs | 
| Nature | Government-issued bonds linked to gold prices; pays fixed interest | Exchange-traded funds backed by physical gold; traded like stocks | 
| Backing | Government of India and RBI | Physical gold stored by fund houses (99.5% purity) | 
| Liquidity | Moderate; tradable but limited volume | High; can be traded anytime on stock exchanges | 
| Taxation | Capital gains exempt after 8 years; interest taxable | LTCG taxed at 20% with indexation; no interest income | 
| Lock-in | 8 years (early exit after 5) | No lock-in; full flexibility | 
Returns, Costs, and Tax Implications
Fixed Interest vs Market-Linked Returns
SGBs provide 2.5% fixed annual interest, adding to capital gains from gold
price movements. Gold ETFs, by contrast, only reflect market price changes
without additional fixed returns.
Capital Gains and Charges
- SGBs: Tax-exempt after 8 years; interest taxed as per income slab.
- ETFs: LTCG taxed at 20% with indexation after 3 years; short-term gains taxed at income slab rates.

· Cash Management Bills (CMBs)
Cash Management
Bills (CMBs) are short-term debt instruments issued by the government to
effectively manage temporary cash flow mismatches. CMBs have a maturity period
typically under 91 days, making them ideal for quick funding solutions. They
are issued as needed, based on the government’s immediate financial
requirements, ensuring efficient cash management. CMBs serve a crucial role in
providing flexibility for addressing short-term funding needs. This allows the
government to maintain fiscal stability. 
· Inflation Indexed Bonds
Inflation-indexed
bonds are tailored to protect your principal investment from the adverse
effects of inflation. Their principal and interest amount is adjusted according
to a recognised inflation index, such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI). This
adjustment ensures that as inflation increases, the value of your principal
rises correspondingly. This helps maintain your investment’s purchasing power
over time. By providing this safeguard, inflation-indexed bonds enable you to
secure real returns. This mitigates the risk of erosion due to inflation. 
· Sovereign Gold Bonds
Sovereign
Gold Bonds (SGBs) are government-backed securities issued by the RBI on behalf
of the Indian government. SGBs are denominated in grams of gold, and the
investment is linked to the price of gold, offering returns based on the
prevailing market rates. SGBs also provide a fixed annual interest rate of
2.5%, which is paid semi-annually. The bonds have a maturity period of 8 years,
with an option to exit after 5 years. Moreover, SGBs are exempt from capital
gains tax if held until maturity, making them a tax-efficient investment. These
bonds can be easily traded on stock exchanges, adding liquidity to the
investment. Sovereign Gold Bonds are a safe, cost-effective option for
investors looking to diversify their portfolios with gold, offering both capital
appreciation and regular income while avoiding the risks of holding physical
gold.
· STRIPs
Separate Trading
of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities (STRIPS) is a unique
financial instrument that allows you to invest in individual components of
government securities. In traditional bonds, both the interest (coupon
payments) and the principal are bundled together. However, with STRIPS, these
components are separated, allowing you to trade them independently.
Essentially, STRIPS splits a bond into two parts—one for the interest payments
and one for the principal repayment at maturity.
· Bonds with Call/ Put Options
When you invest in a bond with a Call option, the issuer can redeem the bond before its maturity date, usually when interest rates fall.

providing flexibility for addressing short-term funding needs. This allows the
government to maintain fiscal stability. 
· Inflation Indexed Bonds
Inflation-indexed
bonds are tailored to protect your principal investment from the adverse
effects of inflation. Their principal and interest amount is adjusted according
to a recognised inflation index, such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI). This
adjustment ensures that as inflation increases, the value of your principal
rises correspondingly. This helps maintain your investment’s purchasing power
over time. By providing this safeguard, inflation-indexed bonds enable you to
secure real returns. This mitigates the risk of erosion due to inflation. 
· Sovereign Gold Bonds
Sovereign
Gold Bonds (SGBs) are government-backed securities issued by the RBI on behalf
of the Indian government. SGBs are denominated in grams of gold, and the
investment is linked to the price of gold, offering returns based on the
prevailing market rates. SGBs also provide a fixed annual interest rate of
2.5%, which is paid semi-annually. The bonds have a maturity period of 8 years,
with an option to exit after 5 years. Moreover, SGBs are exempt from capital
gains tax if held until maturity, making them a tax-efficient investment. These
bonds can be easily traded on stock exchanges, adding liquidity to the
investment. Sovereign Gold Bonds are a safe, cost-effective option for
investors looking to diversify their portfolios with gold, offering both capital
appreciation and regular income while avoiding the risks of holding physical
gold.

Separate Trading
of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities (STRIPS) is a unique
financial instrument that allows you to invest in individual components of
government securities. In traditional bonds, both the interest (coupon
payments) and the principal are bundled together. However, with STRIPS, these
components are separated, allowing you to trade them independently.
Essentially, STRIPS splits a bond into two parts—one for the interest payments
and one for the principal repayment at maturity.

interest rates. By offering the potential for competitive returns in such

Loans (SDLs) are financial instruments issued by individual state governments

title: Green Bonds in India: Sustainable Investments in India to Grow
content:
In recent
years, the conversation around global warming and climate change has taken centre
stage, and for crucial reasons. In their interaction with this conversation,
businesses and governments have sought to address the shortcomings of the
prevalent system through a shift to environment-friendly solutions to the needs
of the environment and the populations they cater to. And thus, we have
observed a marked shift towards sustainable options like electric vehicles,
paperless businesses, infrastructural projects pertaining to solar use and the
like. While the jury is still out on the actual impact of these changes, it is
certain that they have significantly impacted policy designs curated by
governments and corporations alike. Importantly, since a number of these
initiatives demand large scale alterations in the production process, governments
and corporations have sought to facilitate the influx of funds required for the
same through a number of financial instruments - like [green bonds](https://altifi.ai/sign_up).
The idea behind such an initiative is to incentivize investors, corporations and governments to shift towards options that purportedly promote sustainable living and environmental well-being, without compromising on macroeconomic growth, company performances and profit margins and the investors’ financial health.
Background
While the first green bond was issued by the World Bank in 2008, their proliferation in India was observed only since the second half of the last decade. Fast forward to 2023, green bond issuances in India have crossed the $21 billion mark, with the private sector contributing towards 84% of these issuances. The employment of green bonds to fund multiple wind power, hydro power and solar power projects by Greenko Group, the largest bond issuer in India, is a notable example in this respect.
While private
players, as mentioned, dominate issuances pertaining to [green bonds](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) at present, recent policy
decisions imply that the government’s interest in entering the segment. In
2021, a local civic body in Ghaziabad became the first government body to issue
a green bond worth $20 million, thereby marking the state’s foray into the
sub-sector. Later, in January 2023, the government issued sovereign green bonds
worth $980 million, thereby reaffirming its engagement with the medium.
What You Should Know
From how much is known, at present, it is ideal to consider the following factors before making up your mind regarding green bonds:
Diversification & Risk Mitigation

investing in green bonds allows us to add yet another [investment](https://altifi.ai/sign_up) type to your [portfolio](https://altifi.ai/sign_up), it lucidly aids the investors’
pursuit of diversifying our finances.

title: Healthy bond portfolio with Altifi | A bond investment platform
content:
Factors to consider while building a healthy bond portfolio
The investing community is witnessing a purple patch with many asset classes performing well. Stocks, bonds, gold, and real estate are all looking up and creating a feel-good environment.
However, the rich valuations and high asset prices are loaded with the possibility of impending volatility which can be unnerving for investors, especially for those with low-risk appetite. Many investors may be becoming cautious despite the good times being witnessed now and feeling tense at the possibility of downside risk to the portfolio in case things turn for the worse. Signs of volatility have already been witnessed on and off in the stock markets.
While enjoying the current wealth creation run, one cannot ignore the fact that the world is witnessing fast-paced developments that can alter the feel-good factor anytime. There are elections in many key countries in 2024 including India and the US. The volatile geo-political scenario with two major conflicts going on is adding to the worries of investors. Major maritime trade routes are facing problems. Any escalation of the conflicts can create supply chain disruptions and add to inflation pushing back the anticipated rate cut cycles by central banks.
Against this backdrop, it is natural for investors to look for safety and stability of their portfolio in case adverse events impact the riskier asset classes. A good way to limit the downside amid volatility is to increase one’s overall allocation to [bonds](https://altifi.ai/) as In the realm of [investment strategies](https://altifi.ai/), building a bond portfolio stands as a pillar of stability amid the ebb and flow of financial markets. A bond portfolio comprises a collection of fixed income securities, such as government bonds, corporate bonds, and other debt instruments, designed to provide steady returns and mitigate risk. As investors navigate the dynamic landscape of asset classes, including stocks, real estate, and commodities, the allure of bonds becomes increasingly apparent. However, crafting a robust bond portfolio requires careful consideration of various factors to align with individual financial goals and risk appetites.
Assessing Financial Goals & Risk Appetite:
Before diving into the intricacies of bond investments, investors must first embark on a journey of self-assessment, evaluating their financial goals and risk appetite. This introspective process serves as the bedrock upon which a well-structured bond portfolio is built. The key question to ask is how much the allocation to each asset class should be. The mix would vary from person to person. Some of the major financial goals in one’s lifetime are children’s education, purchasing a home, marriage of children and providing for retirement expenses.
The farther the goal, the higher can be allocation to riskier assets such as stock to build a corpus for the milestone.

content:
The key question to ask is how much the allocation to each asset class should be. The mix would vary from person to person. Some of the major financial goals in one’s lifetime are children’s education, purchasing a home, marriage of children and providing for retirement expenses.
The farther the goal, the higher can be allocation to riskier assets such as stock to build a corpus for the milestone. For instance, individuals allocating funds for retirement in the distant future may feel more comfortable allocating a larger proportion of their portfolio to riskier assets, such as equities, in pursuit of higher returns. However, those with a short-term financial goal such as arranging down payment for purchase of a car in the next couple of years may prioritize investing bonds and other fixed income alternatives to minimize volatility.
Furthermore, the risk profile of the investor also plays a key role in [asset allocation](https://altifi.ai/) decisions. For most conservative investors and even moderate risk takers volatility is a bad word. A larger chunk of investments of moderate or low risk investors’ portfolios should go towards fixed income investments, including bonds.
Assessing Income & Accumulation Needs:
Understanding the cash flow requirements associated with various financial goals is important, as it informs the selection of fixed income instruments tailored to meet these needs. Different [financial goals](https://altifi.ai/) may call for differentiated cash flows. title: High Yield vs Low Yield Bonds: Key Differences Explained
content:
Navigating the Spectrum: High Yield vs. Low Yield Bonds
High yield bond or low yield bond, where do I invest? If you are stuck in such a dilemma, you aren’t alone. Believe it or not, it confuses even seasoned bond investors. Although not as dynamic as stocks and equities, bonds have their peculiarities that can make one contemplate. For instance, [high yield bonds](https://altifi.ai/) are exciting concerning returns. But they may be risky. On the other hand, low yield bonds have higher ratings and reliability. However, they may not yield as much. So, having said that, let’s look at some key differences between high yield and low yield bonds to clear the fog.
What are Bonds?
Bonds are debt securities that governments or corporations raise to fund a particular need like project completion, infrastructure development, etc. Thus, when you buy a [bond](https://altifi.ai/bonds), you are lending money to the issuer. In return, the issuer provides periodic interest payments called coupon payments and the principal amount upon maturity. Usually, bonds offer a fixed interest rate, a particular maturity date, and a face value - the amount the bondholder will receive upon the maturity of the bond.
Bonds are a popular investment avenue as they are considered fixed-income securities. This is because bonds provide a fixed and predictable stream of income to investors. Usually, investors deem bonds safer than stocks as the risk level associated with a bond is lower than many other investment options. However, it should be noted that a bond’s security depends on the issuer’s creditworthiness and many internal and external factors.
Depending on who issues them, bonds are broadly categorized as corporate bonds, government bonds, municipal bonds, etc. However, the investment market also classifies them as high yield and low yield. Each has its unique characteristics every aspiring bond investor stuck between the choice of [high yield and low yield bond](https://altifi.ai/bonds) should know.
What are High Yield Bonds?
Also called junk bonds, high yield bonds are fixed-income securities issued by companies with lower credit ratings than investment-grade bonds. Their low credit ratings make them high risk investments. However, these bonds offer higher yields to compensate for the increased default risk of the issuer's lower credit quality stemming from unstable cash flows, high debt levels, or a poor credit record.
What are Low Yield Bonds?
Low yield bonds are bonds that offer a lower interest or return rate. These bonds are issued by companies with a higher rating. Hence, they carry a lower default risk. Although the yield isn't as high, these bonds can prove a prudent choice for investors looking for less risky avenues and a low, yet stable income.
High Yield Bonds vs. Low yield Bonds – Key Differences

title: High Yield vs Low Yield Bonds: Key Differences Explained
content:
Low yield bonds are bonds that offer a lower interest or return rate. These bonds are issued by companies with a higher rating. Hence, they carry a lower default risk. Although the yield isn't as high, these bonds can prove a prudent choice for investors looking for less risky avenues and a low, yet stable income.
High Yield Bonds vs. Low yield Bonds – Key Differences
Now that we’ve looked at the basic definition of high yield bonds and low yield bonds, let’s look at some key differences between them.
| Aspect | High Yield Bonds | Low Yield Bonds | 
| Yield | The yield is higher. Hence, they are called high yield bonds. | The yield is usually lower than high yield bonds. Hence, the bonds are called low yield bonds. | 
| Investment Risk | The investment risk is higher as the company offers a high yield to compensate for the low ratings and the high default risk. | The investment risk is lower as these bonds are issued by entities with a higher credit rating and therefore a lower default risk. | 
| Target Investors | Investors looking to take risks and earn potentially higher returns. | Investors looking for more stability and safety, rather than high returns. | 
| Liquidity | Less liquid than investment-grade bonds. | More liquid on account of higher demand and the stability of the issuer. | 
| Value Sensitivity | Higher sensitivity to interest rate changes and economic conditions. | Lower sensitivity to interest rate and the economic environment. | 
| Issuers | High yield bonds are issued by small or mid-sized companies. | Low-yield bonds are issued by larger or more established companies. | 
| Coupon Payments | High yield bonds usually offer higher coupon payments to compensate for the increased risk. | Low yield bonds offer lower coupon payments on account of the lower risk involved. | 
Are High Yield Bonds Better than Low Yield Bonds?
We wish we could give a straightforward answer to your question. However, you cannot consider a high yield option better than the lower one or vice versa. It depends upon your financial objectives and the extent to which you are prepared to take the risk. For instance, if you are an investor looking for high returns and have a significant corpus to compensate for the risk, you may invest in a high yield bond and stand a chance to earn potentially higher returns over a period. However, on the other hand, if you are looking for a stable income, even if it is a relatively low yield, you may choose low yield bonds.
Ratings of High Yield and Low Yield Bonds
Now, you must be wondering how do you know if a bond is high yield or low yield. One of the most significant indicators to figure it out is the bond ratings. However, it should be noted that bond ratings are indicative and do not guarantee the yield or the fate of a particular bond or its issuer.

title: How To Assess The Risk Reward Balance In Bond Investments | AltiFi
content:
Introduction
Understanding the
balance between [risk and reward](https://altifi.ai/sign_up?utm_source=Website&utm_medium=Homepage&utm_campaign=blog) is essential for making informed investment
decisions. Investing in bonds tends to offer a more straightforward relationship
between risk and potential returns compared to other investment types. Here,
we'll simplify the key risk parameters to consider, helping you navigate your
investment choices wisely.
Parameters
For bond investments, while there are multiple types of risk, the two major ones are (a) volatility risk and (b) credit risk or default risk. Volatility risk, also known as market risk or interest rate risk, arises from daily fluctuations in bond yields influenced by economic events. A bond's price and its yield move inversely: if yields decrease, bond prices increase, and vice versa. A bond’s susceptibility to interest rate changes is measured by its modified duration. Simply put, modified duration shows how much a bond's price is likely to change when interest rates move by 1%. The higher a bond’s duration, the more sensitive it is to shifts in yield. As an example, if yield level in the market comes down by 1%, the price of a bond with modified duration of 4 years would move from Rs 100 to 104. For the same yield movement, price of a bond with modified duration of 2 years would move from Rs 100 to Rs 102.
Credit risk, on the other hand, involves
the possibility of not receiving scheduled payments, including both interest
and principal. This risk is assessed by credit ratings provided by rating
agencies, with AAA being the highest, indicating the lowest risk. It
is easy for you to gauge; the data on credit rating is available on the
[bond](https://altifi.ai/sign_up?utm_source=Website&utm_medium=Homepage&utm_campaign=blog)-related documents as well as on the websites of the rating agencies.
Assessment
On volatility risk, longer the residual (remaining) maturity, higher is the modified duration, hence higher the potential price volatility. It works both ways. For a longer maturity / longer duration bond, when yields come down, you gain more but lose more when yields move up. In a shorter maturity bond, while you gain relatively less when yield come down, you lose relatively less when yields move up.
The bond market often reflects a clearer relationship between risk and reward compared to equities or commodities. Depending on your risk tolerance and investment timeframe, you can select bonds with durations that match your comfort level. At any point, market sentiment—whether bullish or bearish—tends to move bond yields uniformly, though the extent can vary between types, like government versus corporate bonds.
Credit risk, as
mentioned earlier, is assessed by the credit rating.

Long-term financial planning should include making plans for a steady income after one retires. Many investors think of bonds as part of this planning because they have fixed maturity dates, structured cash flows, and set interest payments. If an individual uses them wisely, bonds can help make a steady income that will help pay the bills every month after retirement.
Bonds work on terms that are agreed upon when they are issued, unlike market-linked instruments. Knowing the interest rates, payment frequency, and maturity dates ahead of time can make it easier to plan for the income. This article talks about how bonds are often used to build a monthly pension, the main steps involved, and the things that are usually thought about when setting up this kind of plan.
How Can Investors Build a Monthly Pension Using Bonds: Key Steps
The following are a few steps that investors may use to build a monthly pension using bonds.
Step 1: Evaluate the Monthly Financial Requirement
The first step towards building a monthly pension using bonds is evaluating post-retirement financial requirements. This involves assessing potential expenses and identifying the amount of monthly cash flow that may be required post retirement. Key considerations may include:
- Day-to-day household needs
- Estimated lifestyle-related expenses
- Healthcare expenses
- Potential increase in expenses due to inflation
Having a defined monthly target may help determine the capital required for a bond-based retirement plan.
Step 2. Build a Retirement Corpus During Working Years
Building a monthly pension using bonds generally requires sufficient capital accumulation before retirement. Regular investments during earning years may create a foundation for future cash flow requirements.
Some approaches that may be considered include:
- Allocating a fixed portion of savings towards bond investments
- Selecting cumulative bond options, where available, to benefit from compounding
- Reinvesting periodic bond payments into other fixed-income instruments when cumulative options are unavailable
Gradual accumulation over time may support long-term retirement planning objectives.
Step 3: Set Up a Bond Ladder for Scheduled Payments
A bond ladder involves investing in bonds with different tenures instead of allocating all capital to a single maturity date. Under this approach, bonds mature at different intervals, creating periodic access to invested capital.
This structure may offer the following benefits:
- Maturing bonds may provide cash that can be utilised for retirement-related expenses
- Amounts received upon maturity may be reinvested based on prevailing interest rate conditions
- Staggered maturities may reduce the impact of investing all capital during a single interest-rate environment
A bond ladder may support the creation of relatively consistent cash flows over an extended period.
Step 4: Gradual Transition from Wealth Accumulation to Income Generation
During the early stages of retirement planning, investors may focus on capital accumulation. As retirement approaches, some investors may gradually transition towards bonds that provide periodic payments.
Examples may include:
- Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) bonds with fixed coupon structures

Step 4: Gradual Transition from Wealth Accumulation to Income Generation
During the early stages of retirement planning, investors may focus on capital accumulation. As retirement approaches, some investors may gradually transition towards bonds that provide periodic payments.
Examples may include:
- Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) bonds with fixed coupon structures
- [Corporate bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/corporate-bonds) issued by companies, including Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)
This transition may convert accumulated investments into a stream of periodic payments that can be used for retirement-related expenses.
Step 5: Regularly Monitor and Adjust Investments
Market conditions, interest rates, and financial requirements may change over time. Periodic reviews may help ensure that a bond portfolio remains aligned with retirement objectives.
Important review considerations may include:
- Assessing bond investments annually or when financial requirements change
- Reviewing issuer credit ratings
- Monitoring interest rate movements and maturity distribution
Regular portfolio reviews may assist in maintaining alignment between investment allocations and retirement planning requirements.
Some Tips on Building a Monthly Pension Using Bonds
The following are some useful points that
Focus on Capital Preservation Near Retirement
As the retirement time comes closer, capital preservation may become a more significant consideration. Bond selection may therefore focus on issuer quality and creditworthiness.
Commonly considered categories include:
- Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) bonds
- Government Securities (G-Secs)
- AAA-rated corporate bonds
- AA-rated corporate bonds
Higher-rated bonds may carry comparatively lower credit risk than lower-rated alternatives.
Diversify Investments Across Different Bond Issuers and Tenures
Concentrating investments in a single issuer or maturity may increase portfolio risk. Diversification across issuers and tenures may contribute to a more balanced bond portfolio.
Diversification may help by:
- Reducing issuer-specific credit risk
- Creating relatively smoother payment flows
- Supporting portfolio stability during changing market conditions
A diversified approach may strengthen retirement-focused bond allocations.
Gradually Increase Bond Allocations as Income Rises
As earnings increase over time, investment contributions may also be reviewed periodically. Increasing allocations towards bonds may support long-term retirement planning goals.
Some approaches may include:
- Increasing bond investments following salary revisions
- Allocating bonuses or other surplus funds towards fixed-income investments
- Directing excess savings into bond investments where appropriate
Regular contribution increases may support capital accumulation over longer investment horizons.
Review Credit Ratings Before Investing
Credit ratings indicate the creditworthiness of bond issuers and their ability to meet repayment obligations. Reviewing ratings may form an important part of bond selection.
The rating categories include:
- AAA: Highest credit quality with the lowest credit risk
- AA: Very high credit quality with comparatively low credit risk
- A: High credit quality with adequate capacity to meet obligations
- BBB: Adequate credit quality with increasing sensitivity to adverse conditions

title: How Bonds Can Create a Monthly Pension Income
content:
Reviewing ratings may form an important part of bond selection.
The rating categories include:
- AAA: Highest credit quality with the lowest credit risk
- AA: Very high credit quality with comparatively low credit risk
- A: High credit quality with adequate capacity to meet obligations
- BBB: Adequate credit quality with increasing sensitivity to adverse conditions
- BB: Speculative grade with elevated credit risk
- B: Higher speculative risk and increased vulnerability to adverse conditions
- CCC: Very high credit risk with significant uncertainty regarding repayment
- CC: Very high likelihood of default
- C: Extremely high credit risk and potential default concerns
- D: In default or expected to default on obligations
Focusing on credit quality may assist investors in evaluating the risk profile of bonds used for retirement planning.
Estimating How Much Money You Need Each Month
To plan a monthly pension with bonds, an individual first needs to know how much capital they might need after they retire. This usually means figuring out how much capital they need to spend on things like groceries, healthcare, insurance, and other things that are part of daily life. Inflation is another important factor to think about because costs usually go up over time.
Knowing how much capital one may need to live comfortably each month can help individuals figure out how much capital they need to invest and what kinds of bonds might be suitable for making a regular income.
Using Bond Maturities to Help Pay for Regular Expenses
The idea of a bond ladder is a common way to plan for retirement income. This means buying several bonds that will mature at different times instead of investing all of the capital into one bond.
With staggered maturities, some of the capital that an individual has invested becomes available at set times. Individuals can either use these earnings to pay bills or reinvest them, depending on how much capital they need and what the current interest rates are. This structure can help lower the risk of reinvestment and make individuals less dependent on when interest rates rise.
Things to Consider When Using Bonds for Pension
Diversification is a key way to lower risk. Having bonds from different issuers and with different maturities helps individuals not put too much capital into one borrower or time period. This can help make income streams more stable.
As retirement gets closer, people often think about how to protect their capital. To lower credit-related risks, people may choose higher-quality bonds, like government securities or highly rated instruments. Credit ratings give individuals a way to analyse how well the issuer can pay back loans and interest.
It's also common to reevaluate contributions as income levels change over the course of a person's working life. One can reach their long-term income goals by slowly increasing their bond allocations without putting too much stress on their finances.
Conclusion
Bonds may help investors plan for retirement by giving them a structured and predictable way to make capital.
