title: Tax on Sovereign Gold Bonds
content:
According to the Reserve Bank of India Annual Report 2025–26, Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) continued to remain part of India’s gold-linked savings framework even after fresh issuances were paused in recent periods. Gold prices also remained elevated through 2025 due to central bank purchases, inflation concerns, and geopolitical uncertainty. Against this backdrop, many first-time investors are reviewing how tax on sovereign gold bonds works before entering the secondary market.
Understanding SGB tax matters because taxation can affect the final post-tax outcome, even when the underlying asset tracks gold prices.
What are Sovereign Gold Bonds?
[Sovereign Gold Bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/sovereign-gold-bond) (SGBs) are government securities issued by the Reserve Bank of India on behalf of the Government of India. Instead of buying physical gold, investors purchase bonds denominated in grams of gold, with returns linked to the prevailing market price of gold.
Each SGB is issued at a fixed subscription price and carries a maturity period of eight years, with an early redemption option available from the fifth year onwards on designated interest payment dates. At maturity, investors receive the equivalent value of the gold based on prevailing market prices.
In addition to potential gains from rising gold prices, SGB investors earn a fixed interest rate of 2.50% per annum on the initial investment amount. According to the Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme terms notified by the Reserve Bank of India, these reference terms remained unchanged in 2026, although future revisions may occur subject to regulatory directives.
Unlike [corporate bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/corporate-bonds), SGBs are backed by the Government of India and therefore generally carry relatively lower default risk compared to debt instruments issued by private companies.
How Tax on SGB Works
Tax treatment differs depending on whether an investor holds the bond until maturity, exits early, or sells it on the secondary market. This difference could directly affect the applicable tax liability.
Tax on Interest Income
SGBs pay a 2.50% annual coupon, credited semi-annually. Interest earned from SGBs is taxable under “Income from Other Sources”. This reflects standard taxation rules applicable to coupon income from government securities.
As a result, investors may need to add this interest income to their total taxable income and pay tax according to their applicable slab rate. For example, if an investor earns ₹5,000 as annual coupon income, this amount may be taxed at the individual’s marginal tax rate.
So in SGBs, investors receive scheduled coupon payments irrespective of gold price movement. However, the interest is fully taxable and may reduce net post-tax income, especially for investors in higher tax brackets.

content:
For example, if an investor earns ₹5,000 as annual coupon income, this amount may be taxed at the individual’s marginal tax rate.
So in SGBs, investors receive scheduled coupon payments irrespective of gold price movement. However, the interest is fully taxable and may reduce net post-tax income, especially for investors in higher tax brackets.
Worth noting, no Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) applies on SGB interest, but tax liability may still arise at the time of filing returns.
Tax on Redemption at Maturity
This is one of the most discussed aspects of the SGB tax. Capital gains arising on redemption of Sovereign Gold Bonds at maturity are exempt for individual investors. This tax exemption exists under Section 47 of the Income Tax Act for eligible redemptions.
As a result, if an investor holds the bond for the full eight-year tenure and redeems directly with the issuer, any appreciation linked to gold prices is not subject to capital gains tax. For example, if an investor purchased SGBs at ₹5,500 per gram and redeemed them at ₹9,200 per gram, the difference may remain exempt, subject to prevailing tax law.
So, maturity redemption may improve post-tax outcomes, subject to holding period and prevailing tax rules. But investors need to need to hold until maturity period or until maturity date.
Tax on Premature Exit Through Exchange Sale
SGBs are listed on the secondary market through exchanges such as the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) and the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) Limited. The secondary market refers to the platform where investors buy and sell existing securities after issuance.
If investors sell SGBs before maturity on the exchange, capital gains tax may apply. This is driven by the fact that exchange transactions are treated differently from sovereign redemption. As a result, taxation usually depends on the holding period.
Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG)
If sold before 12 months, gains may be taxed according to the applicable income slab. So investors can access liquidity before maturity. However, tax liability may reduce effective proceeds.
Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG)
If Sovereign Gold Bonds are sold on the secondary market after the applicable holding period, long-term capital gains provisions may apply under prevailing tax rules.?
However, SGBs are not taxed in the same manner as physical gold or gold ETFs in all cases. For individual investors, capital gains arising on redemption at maturity are currently exempt from tax. In contrast, gains realised from sale on the exchange may be subject to capital gains tax based on the holding period and applicable provisions at the time of sale.
Price Movement and Tax Impact in the Secondary Market
SGBs may trade at a premium or discount to their intrinsic gold value. Exchange prices can differ from underlying gold prices.

Price Movement and Tax Impact in the Secondary Market
SGBs may trade at a premium or discount to their intrinsic gold value. Exchange prices can differ from underlying gold prices. This is driven by liquidity, demand-supply mismatch, and time remaining to maturity.
As a result, investors buying from the secondary market may purchase below or above the fair value. For example, an SGB nearing maturity may trade closer to prevailing gold value, while long-duration bonds may reflect wider pricing gaps.
Duration refers to a bond’s sensitivity to interest rate changes and time horizon. Although duration is more relevant in conventional fixed-income securities, longer residual maturity may still affect secondary market pricing behaviour in SGBs.

How SGBs Compare with Fixed Deposits (FDs) From a Tax Perspective

An FD is a deposit product where funds remain locked for a defined tenure and earn a pre-agreed interest rate. Interest from fixed deposits is generally fully taxable annually. This reflects standard deposit taxation norms. As a result, investors may pay tax each year regardless of whether they withdraw proceeds.
Fixed Deposits (FDs) are simpler to understand, with interest taxed as per the investor’s slab rate. This clarity comes with the drawback that taxable interest may reduce the net realised return.
By contrast, SGB maturity gains for eligible investors may remain exempt if held until redemption. title: Sovereign Gold Bond vs Physical Gold vs Digital Gold
content:
For many years, Indian households have chosen to invest in gold. Investors now have a choice between Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) and physical gold. Although exposure to gold prices is offered by both choices, there are differences in terms of returns, taxes, expenses, liquidity, and ease. Both options serve different investor needs, making it important to understand their features before investing.
What is a Sovereign Gold Bond (SGB)?
A Sovereign Gold Bond is a government-backed investment linked to the value of gold in grams. SGBs are issued by the RBI on behalf of the Indian government. One gram of gold is represented by each unit, which is connected to the market price of 999-purity gold.
SGBs have an 8-year maturity term, however, starting in the fifth year, there is an early redemption option. These bonds are held electronically by investors, eliminating the need for physical storage.
The set interest rate of 2.50% yearly on the initial investment amount, paid semi-annually, is a crucial component of SGBs. As a result, investors benefit from both interest income and any increases in the price of gold.
Fresh Sovereign Gold Bond issuances have been discontinued by the Government of India. However, new investors can currently acquire SGBs only through the secondary market, subject to market availability and liquidity.
Investing in Sovereign Gold Bonds
Investing in [Sovereign Gold Bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/sovereign-gold-bond) is a simple process for most investors. These bonds could previously be purchased during new RBI issuances or through stock exchanges after listing. As fresh SGB issuances have been discontinued, investors can currently buy existing bonds only through stock exchanges.
The application process requires completing KYC formalities, with PAN being mandatory. Investors must specify the quantity they wish to purchase and make the payment through approved channels. After the purchase is completed, the bonds are credited to the investor's Demat account.
Pros of Investing in SGBs
SGBs offer several advantages beyond simple exposure to gold prices.
- Interest Income: SGBs pay a fixed interest of 2.50% annually on the original investment amount. This interest is paid semi-annually and continues throughout the bond tenure.
- Additional Return Potential: Unlike physical gold, Gold ETFs, or gold mutual funds, SGBs provide recurring income in addition to any increase in gold prices.
- Tax Advantages: Capital gains earned when SGBs are redeemed at maturity are exempt from Long-Term Capital Gains tax.
- Zero Storage Cost: Since SGBs are held electronically, investors do not incur locker charges, insurance expenses, or theft-related concerns.
- No Making Charges: Investors gain gold exposure without paying making charges commonly associated with jewellery purchases.

title: Step-Up Bonds: Meaning, Benefits, Risks and Working Explained
content:
Step-up bonds are debt instruments where the coupon rate increases at predetermined intervals during the bond tenure. Unlike conventional bonds which carry the same coupon rate throughout their life, step-up bonds have a pre-defined coupon escalation schedule disclosed at issuance. This allows investors to understand how coupon payments may change over the tenure before making an investment decision. Understanding how step-up bonds work, their key features, associated risks, and credit considerations is important when evaluating these instruments within the broader corporate bond market.
What are Step-Up Bonds?
A step-up bond is a debt instrument whose coupon rate increases incrementally at predefined, regular intervals over its tenure. Unlike floating-rate bonds that fluctuate based on market-linked benchmarks, the timing and extent of rate increase in a step-up bond are disclosed in the information memorandum at the time of issuance. This structure provides visibility regarding future coupon adjustments, allowing investors to review potential payment schedules from the outset.
How Step-Up Bonds Work
When a company issues a step-up bond, the scheduling of the coupon increases is contractually defined. For instance, consider a company issuing a seven-year step-up bond with a face value of ₹2,00,000. The The structure may specify an interest rate of 6.80% for years 1–2, 7.60% for years 3–5, and 8.40% for years 6–7. Based on this step-up schedule, the average interest rate works out to 7.60%, while the indicative yield may be around 7.53%, depending on the bond’s price, cash-flow timing, and redemption terms.
Instead of receiving a flat payout, the investor receives a coupon stream that increases over the seven-year tenure. This step-up mechanism may result in a higher weighted average coupon rate than a bond that remains at its initial coupon rate throughout the tenure..
Key Features of Step-Up Bonds
The key features of step-up bonds are as follows:
Predefined Escalation Schedule
Every coupon rate adjustment and the exact date it takes effect are established beforehand, eliminating uncertainty regarding coupon changes during the bond tenure.
Varied Adjustment Triggers
While time-based intervals are the most common trigger, coupon increases can also be linked to external factors, such as changes in the issuer's credit profile or benchmark-linked conditions, depending on the bond structure.
Call Provisions
Many step-up bonds incorporate provisions that may provide the issuing company with the right to redeem the bond before its maturity date.
Benefits of Step-Up Bonds
The benefits of step-up bonds are as follows:
Mitigation of Interest Rate Risk
In a rising interest-rate environment, conventional fixed-rate bonds may experience price pressure. Step-up bonds may partly address this concern because the coupon rate increases according to a predefined schedule.
Coupon Visibility

title: Step-Up Bonds: Meaning, Benefits, Risks and Working Explained
content:
Benefits of Step-Up Bonds
The benefits of step-up bonds are as follows:
Mitigation of Interest Rate Risk
In a rising interest-rate environment, conventional fixed-rate bonds may experience price pressure. Step-up bonds may partly address this concern because the coupon rate increases according to a predefined schedule.
Coupon Visibility
Since the coupon escalation schedule is disclosed at issuance, investors can review future coupon adjustments before investing.
Incremental Cash Flows
The scheduled coupon increases mean that the coupon payments rise over the tenure of the bond.
Step-Up Bonds vs Fixed-Rate Bonds
The following table highlights the key difference between step-up bonds and fixed-rate bonds:
| Factor | Step-Up Bonds | Fixed-Rate Bonds | 
|---|---|---|
| Coupon Structure | Increases at predefined intervals | Remains identical throughout the tenure | 
| Interest Rate Protection | May provide some protection against rising market rates | May face price pressure when market rates rise | 
| Cash Flow Profile | Escalating coupon payments | Fixed coupon payments | 
| Primary Structural Risk | Potential early redemption through call provisions | Reinvestment risk after maturity | 
Risks of Investing in Step-Up Bonds
Step-up bonds involve the following risks.
- Call Risk: A significant risk in step-up bonds is the issuer’s ability to redeem the bond early once coupon rates rise. This deprives investors of the higher scheduled payments.
- Reinvestment Risk: If the bond is called, investors must reinvest the proceeds at prevailing market rates, which may be relatively lower than the step-up schedule promised. This reduces the effective yield compared to what was initially expected.
- Interest Rate Risk: Step-up bonds are traded in secondary markets, so their value fluctuates with broader market interest rates. Rising rates can make even the stepped-up coupons less preferable and reduce bond prices. Whereas, falling rates may increase the chance of early redemption.
- Credit Risk: The issuer’s financial health directly affects repayment capacity. A downgrade reduces bond value and raises default probability. Some structures link coupon hikes to rating downgrades, which compensate investors but simultaneously signal higher risk.
- Liquidity Risk: Not all step-up bonds are actively traded, which means selling before maturity may be difficult or require a reduction in price.
- Complexity Risk: Step-up bonds often involve multiple coupon stages that can be confusing. Understanding the timing and magnitude of increases requires careful reading of the offer documents, making them more complex than plain fixed-rate bonds.
Who Should Invest in Step-Up Bonds?
Step-up bonds are fixed-income instruments that may align with investors having a medium to long-term investment horizon, generally three years or more. These instruments offer coupon payments that increase over time, which may be suitable for investors who prefer gradually rising payouts instead of fixed payments.
When assessing such bonds, attention to the call option feature becomes important, as early redemption by the issuer may impact the expected coupon schedule.

These instruments offer coupon payments that increase over time, which may be suitable for investors who prefer gradually rising payouts instead of fixed payments.
When assessing such bonds, attention to the call option feature becomes important, as early redemption by the issuer may impact the expected coupon schedule.
These instruments may not be suitable for those expecting stable and uniform coupon payments or where early exit flexibility is a key requirement.
Conclusion
Step-up bonds represent a structured category of corporate debt where coupon rates increase according to a predefined schedule during the bond tenure. The coupon escalation mechanism distinguishes them from conventional fixed-rate bonds and provides visibility into future payment structures. However, features such as call provisions, liquidity considerations, inflation risk, and issuer credit quality remain important factors for evaluation. Reviewing the coupon schedule, redemption terms, and credit profile of the issuing company may support a more informed assessment of how these instruments operate.
FAQs
How are step-up bonds different from regular bonds?
Regular bonds maintain the same coupon rate throughout their tenure, whereas step-up bonds feature scheduled coupon increases at predetermined intervals.
Do step-up bonds always provide higher returns?
No. Actual returns may vary based on purchase price, call provisions, market conditions, coupon structure, and the issuer's repayment performance.
What is call risk in a step-up bond?
Call risk refers to the possibility that the issuing company redeems the bond before maturity, ending future scheduled coupon increases.
Are step-up bonds suitable for long-term investors?
The suitability of step-up bonds depends on factors such as investment objectives, tenure requirements, call provisions, and issuer credit quality.

title: What Are Strip Bonds? Meaning, Features, Benefits & Risks Explained

Strip bonds are fixed-income instruments created by separating a bond's coupon payments from its principal repayment. Each component then trades individually as a zero-coupon security, purchased at a discount and repaid at face value when it matures. Strip bonds provide a mechanism for investors considering fixed-income choices to lock in a known future value without worrying about reinvestment.
What are Strip Bonds?
Strip bonds are zero-coupon securities that have their principle and interest installments offered separately.
Periodic interest is not paid on a zero-coupon bond. Instead, when it matures, it is redeemed at face value after being purchased at a discount. The return comes from the difference between the purchase price and the maturity value.
For example, a 10-year government bond with semi-annual coupons can be split into twenty coupon strips and one main strip. Every component turns into a separate security with its own market price and maturity date.
How Does Bond Stripping Work?
Bond stripping separates a coupon-bearing bond into individual cash flow components that may be traded independently.
In India, this facility applies to selected government securities identified by the RBI.
Step-by-Step: From Coupon Bond to Stripped Security
The process generally follows these steps:
Step 1: RBI identifies eligible government security.
Step 2: A holder submits a stripping request.
Step 3: Coupon payments and principal repayment are separated.
Step 4: Individual strips are credited as separate securities.
Step 5: Each strip may be traded independently.
Step 6: Strips may later be recombined into the original bond through reconstitution.
Principal Strip vs. Coupon Strip (Types)
Strip bonds are available in two forms: coupon strips and principal strips. Each type represents a different future payment from the original bond.
| Attribute | Coupon Strip | Principal Strip | 
|---|---|---|
| What it represents | Single interest payment | Final principal repayment | 
| Face value | Equal to coupon amount | Equal to original face value | 
| Maturity date | Original coupon payment date | Original redemption date | 
| Duration | Shorter | Longest among all strips | 
| Price sensitivity | Lower | Higher | 
| Typical buyer | Investors matching shorter liabilities | Pension funds and insurers | 
How to Calculate Returns / YTM
Strip bonds do not pay regular interest during the investment period. Investors earn returns from the difference between the purchase price and maturity value.
Yield to Maturity (YTM) shows the annual return earned when held until maturity.
The YTM Formula for Zero-Coupon Securities
YTM = (Face Value ÷ Purchase Price)^(1/n) − 1
Where:
Face Value = Amount received at maturity
Purchase Price = Amount invested
n = Years remaining until maturity
A lower purchase price generally results in a higher yield for investors.

So, the Implied YTM: is 7.18% per annum
Advantages of Strip Bonds
Strip bonds offer several features that may benefit investors with long-term financial goals.
- No Reinvestment Risk: Investors do not need to reinvest interest because no coupon payments are received.
- Known Maturity Value: The amount received at maturity is known when the investment is made.
- Useful for Future Goals: Investors can match bond maturity dates with planned financial requirements.
- Simple Structure: Returns depend on one future payment, making valuation easier to understand.
- Government Backing: Government security strips carry the credit quality of the Government of India.
Risks of Strip Bonds
Investors should consider the risks associated with strip bonds before making an investment. Investors may be better able to make wise investing choices if they are aware of these hazards.
- Interest Rate Risk: If market interest rates increase throughout the holding period, prices may drop precipitously.
- Liquidity Risk: In the secondary market, it might occasionally be challenging to find purchasers before maturity.
- No Regular Income: Throughout the investment period, investors do not receive recurring cash flows.
- Inflation Risk: Over time, inflation may lower the real value of proceeds from future maturities.
- Tax Complexity: Compared to certain conventional fixed-income assets, tax treatment may be more complicated.
Tax Treatment in India
The holding period and relevant rules determine how strip bonds are treated tax-wise.

Tax Treatment in India
The holding period and relevant rules determine how strip bonds are treated tax-wise. Bonds sold within a year are typically seen as short-term capital gains. Typically, the investor's applicable income tax bracket determines how these gains are taxed.
Gains on strip bonds that are held for longer than a year are often regarded as long-term capital gains. Subject to present legislation, long-term profits may be taxed at 12.5% without indexation.
TDS may also apply when bond income exceeds prescribed limits. The applicable TDS rate is generally 10% when PAN is provided. The rate may increase to 20% if PAN details are not available.
How to Invest in Strip Bonds
Strip bonds are available for purchase by investors via authorised government securities platforms and intermediaries.
Step 1: Create an account with an authorised broker or RBI Retail Direct.
Step 2: Look for accessible strip bonds and examine the characteristics of their maturity.
Step 3: Before choosing an appropriate bond, evaluate prices, yields, and liquidity.
Step 4: Use the selected investing platform to place the buy order.
The bond can be sold on the secondary market or held until it matures.
Strip Bonds vs. Zero Coupon Bonds
Zero-coupon bonds and strip bonds are similar in that they both don't pay periodic interest.
| Parameter | Strip Bonds | Zero Coupon Bonds | 
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Created from existing coupon-bearing bonds | Usually issued directly as zero-coupon instruments | 
| Interest Payments | None | None | 
| Purchase Method | Created through bond stripping | Issued directly by the issuer | 
| Return Source | Difference between purchase price and maturity value | Difference between purchase price and maturity value | 
| Maturity Structure | Multiple maturity dates | Single maturity date |

The principal and coupon payments of a bond are divided into distinct zero-coupon securities to create strip bonds, which are fixed-income instruments. title: What Are Strip Bonds? Meaning, Features, Benefits & Risks Explained
content:
The suitability of strip bonds depends on an individual's financial objectives, risk tolerance, and investing horizon.
Frequently Asked Questions About Strip Bonds
What is the difference between strip bonds and zero-coupon bonds?
An existing coupon-bearing bond is divided into separate cash flows to generate strip bonds, a kind of zero-coupon bond. Some zero-coupon bonds are issued directly as zero-coupon securities; not all of them are strip bonds.
Are strip bonds available in India?
Yes. For qualified Government of India assets, the RBI implemented the Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal Securities (STRIPS) facility in 2010 to enable trading of strip bonds. These securities are accessible to investors via market intermediaries and authorised platforms.
What is the minimum investment amount for strip bonds?
Although real investment requirements vary depending on the platform, market lot size, and trading conditions, government securities typically have a face value of ₹100.
How are strip bonds different from regular coupon bonds?
Regular bonds restore principal at maturity and pay interest on a regular basis. Strip bonds deliver the maturity value as a single payment at the end of the term and offer no interim payments.
Are strip bonds associated with zero risk?
No. While government-backed strips carry low credit risk, they remain exposed to interest rate risk, liquidity risk, and inflation risk.
What happens when a strip bond matures?
At maturity, the investor receives the face value of the strip bond. The amount is credited through the applicable settlement system.
Can NRIs invest in strip bonds in India?
Subject to RBI norms and FEMA laws, NRIs may invest in government securities. The investment path and current laws determine eligibility.
How are strip bonds taxed compared to fixed deposits?
Interest on fixed deposits is subject to taxation based on the investor's income tax bracket. Depending on the holding duration and relevant rules, strip bonds are typically subject to capital gains taxation. TDS may apply in certain situations.

title: Bond IPO Terms: Essential Definitions Every Investor Should Know
content:
A bond public issue, commonly referred to as a Bond IPO, is a process through which eligible issuers offer bonds or non-convertible debentures (NCDs) to the public for subscription. The process involves multiple intermediaries, regulatory requirements, and instrument-specific terms that investors may encounter across offer documents and application forms. Understanding the terms associated with a bond public issue is crucial for an investor who wants to invest in bonds.
Key Terms Used in a Bond Public Issue
The following are some of the key terms used in a public issue of a bond.
Registrar
The Registrar to the Issue is a SEBI-registered entity that manages the application and allotment process for a bond public issue. Responsibilities typically include processing applications, maintaining investor records, handling allotment, and coordinating refunds where applicable. The Registrar acts as a link between the issuer and investors throughout the issue process.
Debenture Trustee
A Debenture Trustee is a SEBI-registered entity appointed to represent the interests of bondholders. The trustee monitors the issuer's compliance with the terms of the bond, including security creation and covenant adherence. In the event of a default, the Debenture Trustee may initiate action on behalf of bondholders. Appointment of a Debenture Trustee is mandatory for public issues of debt securities in India.
Lead Manager
A Lead Manager, also referred to as a Book Running Lead Manager (BRLM), is a SEBI-registered merchant banker responsible for managing the bond public issue process. Responsibilities include due diligence, preparation of offer documents, coordination with regulators and exchanges, and marketing the issue to potential investors. A single issue may have multiple lead managers depending on its size and structure.
Distributors/Broker
Distributors and brokers are intermediaries that facilitate investor participation in a bond public issue. They facilitate the distribution of the issue across investor segments. Distributors may include banks, non-banking financial companies, and registered brokers empanelled by the issuer or lead managers for the specific issue.
Rating Agencies
Credit rating agencies assess the creditworthiness of the bond issuer and assign a rating to the instrument. In India, SEBI-registered agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, and India Ratings provide these assessments. The rating reflects the agency's opinion on the issuer's ability to meet debt obligations on time. A higher rating generally indicates lower perceived credit risk. Ratings are subject to review and may be revised during the tenure of the instrument.
Application Date
The application date refers to the period during which investors may submit subscription applications for a bond public issue. This window, also referred to as the issue period or subscription period, is specified in the offer document. Applications received outside this window are generally not considered for allotment.
Issue Details

title: Bond IPO Terms: Essential Definitions Every Investor Should Know
content:
Ratings are subject to review and may be revised during the tenure of the instrument.
Application Date
The application date refers to the period during which investors may submit subscription applications for a bond public issue. This window, also referred to as the issue period or subscription period, is specified in the offer document. Applications received outside this window are generally not considered for allotment.
Issue Details
Issue details refer to the key terms and parameters of the bond public issue as disclosed in the offer document. These typically include the issue size, face value, coupon rate, tenor, interest payment frequency, credit rating, objects of the issue, and allotment terms. Investors are generally advised to review issue details in the prospectus or information memorandum before applying.
ASBA
ASBA stands for Application Supported by Blocked Amount. It is a mechanism through which an applicant's subscription amount is blocked in their bank account at the time of application rather than transferred immediately to the issuer. The blocked amount is debited only upon allotment. In cases of partial or non-allotment, the remaining amount is automatically unblocked. ASBA is the standard application mode for public issues of securities in India.
Base Issue
The base issue refers to the minimum fundraising amount that an issuer intends to raise through a bond public issue. In many cases, issuers may retain the option to accept subscriptions beyond the base issue size up to a predefined limit, known as the oversubscription option or greenshoe option. The total amount raised may therefore exceed the base issue size, subject to the terms disclosed in the offer document.
Allotment
Allotment refers to the process of assigning bonds to applicants following the close of the subscription period. Allotment is carried out in accordance with the basis of allotment disclosed in the offer document. In cases of oversubscription, allotment may be proportionate or based on draw of lots, depending on the investor category and applicable regulations. Unallotted amounts are refunded or unblocked through the ASBA mechanism.
Tranche
A tranche is a part of a larger bond issue that is offered to investors separately. An issuer may divide a bond issue into multiple tranches, with each tranche having different features such as maturity period, interest rate, issue date, or investor category. Each tranche is treated as a separate offering for investors.
Investor Categories
Bond public issues in India typically define investor categories to allocate portions of the issue across different subscriber types. Reservations for each category are specified in the offer document.
Institutional Investors
Institutional investors are large organisations that invest money on behalf of their customers, members, or stakeholders. These may include banks, insurance companies, mutual funds, pension funds, and other regulated financial institutions. A specified portion of a bond public issue may be reserved for this category.
Non-Institutional Investors

title: Treasury Bills vs Notes vs Bonds : Explained
content:
Treasury securities are government-issued debt instruments used to raise funds for public spending and ongoing fiscal requirements. [Treasury Bills](https://altifi.ai/bonds/treasury-bills), Treasury Notes, and Treasury Bonds fall within this group, yet they differ in how long they run, how income is structured, and how they react to interest rate changes. These instruments are often associated with relatively lower credit risk because they are backed by the government. At the same time, their market value can shift with changing interest rates. Looking at the difference between treasury bill and treasury note and treasury bonds closely makes it easier to see how each fits into different timeframes and financial situations.
What are Treasury Bills (T-Bills)?
Treasury Bills, usually called T-Bills, are short-term [government securities](https://altifi.ai/bonds/government-securities) issued at a price lower than their face value. They do not pay periodic interest. Instead, the income comes from the difference between what is paid at purchase and what is received at maturity.
In simple terms, an investor buys a T-Bill at a discounted price and receives the full face value when it matures. This gap between the two amounts represents the income. These instruments are generally issued through auctions and are often used to meet short-term funding needs.
Key Features of Treasury Bills
- Short maturity, usually up to one year
- Issued at a discount to face value
- No periodic coupon payments
- Interest income realised at maturity
- Active participation in liquid markets
- Associated with lower credit risk due to government backing
What are Treasury Notes (T-Notes)?
Treasury Notes, or T-Notes, are medium-term government securities that provide periodic interest payments. They are typically issued close to their face value and offer a fixed coupon across the holding period.
They sit between short-term and long-term instruments, which may offer a balance between income generation and interest rate sensitivity. Many times, they are looked at for a balance between coupon income and moderate exposure to interest rate movements. Their market value can move over time, especially when interest rates shift.
Key Features of Treasury Notes
- Medium-term maturity, generally between 2 and 10 years
- Fixed coupon payments, often paid twice a year
- Available for trading in the secondary market
- Moderate sensitivity to interest rate changes
- Provides periodic interest income
What are Treasury Bonds (T-Bonds)?
Treasury Bonds, commonly referred to as T-Bonds, are long-term government securities designed for extended time horizons. They may provide scheduled interest payments over time and return to the principal at maturity, subject to issuer obligations.
These instruments are usually associated with long-duration allocations. Because of their longer maturity, their prices tend to react more to changes in interest rates. Even small shifts in rates can have a noticeable impact on their market value.

They may provide scheduled interest payments over time and return to the principal at maturity, subject to issuer obligations.
These instruments are usually associated with long-duration allocations. Because of their longer maturity, their prices tend to react more to changes in interest rates. Even small shifts in rates can have a noticeable impact on their market value.
Key Features of Treasury Bonds
- Long maturity, typically 20 to 30 years
- Fixed coupon payments throughout the tenure
- Higher sensitivity to interest rate movements

- Used in longer-duration allocation strategies in some cases
Key Differences Between Treasury Bills, Treasury Notes, and Treasury Bonds
A closer comparison helps bring out how these instruments differ in structure, duration, and income pattern.
| Basis | Treasury Bills (T-Bills) | Treasury Notes (T-Notes) | Treasury Bonds (T-Bonds) | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Maturity | Up to 1 year | 2 to 10 years | 20 to 30 years | 
| Income Structure | Discount-based | Fixed coupon | Fixed coupon | 
| Interest Payments | No periodic payments | Semi-annual payments | Semi-annual payments | 
| Price Sensitivity | Lower | Moderate | Higher | 
| Investment Horizon | Short-term | Medium-term | Long-term | 
| Liquidity | Generally high | Generally high | Generally high | 
T-Bills are built for short-term needs. Since there are no interim payments, the entire income is realised at maturity. Their shorter duration also means they are less affected by interest rate changes compared to longer instruments.
T-Notes offer a middle ground. They provide regular coupon income and carry moderate duration. Prices can change over time due to shifts in interest rates, which may impact the market value if sold before maturity.
T-Bonds extend over much longer periods. Because of this, they tend to be more sensitive to interest rate movements. Even a small change in rates can influence their market value. At the same time, they provide periodic coupon payments across a longer span.
How to Buy Treasury Bills, Treasury Notes, and Treasury Bonds
Treasury securities are issued through government auctions conducted by the central authority. Investors can take part directly, where access is available, or go through authorised intermediaries such as banks and financial institutions.
Beyond the primary market, these instruments are also available in the secondary market. This means they can be bought or sold before maturity. Prices in this market may differ from face value and often reflect current interest rate conditions and demand.
The process generally involves opening the required account, submitting identification details, and placing an order through the chosen channel. Settlement follows standard market systems. Minimum allocation requirements and access routes can vary depending on the issuing framework.

title: Types of Government Bonds in India Explained
content:
[Government bonds in India](https://altifi.ai/bonds/government-securities) are debt instruments issued by the Central and State Governments to raise funds for public spending. These are used in areas such as infrastructure development, welfare schemes, and fiscal management. In simple terms, when you invest in a government bond, you are lending funds to the government in return for periodic interest payments and repayment of the principal at maturity. There are many types of government bonds in India. This article explores the different types of government bonds in India.
What are Government Bonds?
Government bonds, or Government Securities in India, are essentially a way for the government to borrow funds from investors. You lend to the government for a fixed period, usually anywhere between 5 and 40 years, and in return, you receive interest at regular intervals along with the principal at maturity.
In practice, these instruments sit at the stable end of the investment spectrum. The sovereign backing makes them highly reliable, which is why many investors use them as a foundation in their portfolio rather than as a growth driver.
Different Types of Government Bonds in India
Once you move beyond the basic definition, the structure starts to vary. Each type of bond is designed with a slightly different purpose in mind.
Fixed-Rate Bonds
These are relatively straightforward. The interest rate stays the same throughout the tenure. Basically, what you see at the start is what you continue to receive. Investors who want clarity in cash flows may prefer these.
Floating Rate Bonds (FRBs)
Here, the interest rate does not stay fixed. It resets at predefined intervals and is usually linked to a benchmark. Worth noting, these tend to work better when interest rates are moving up, since the returns adjust along with the market.
Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs)
They allowing investing in gold without dealing with physical storage. You get returns linked to gold prices along with a fixed interest component. In practice, this makes them useful for diversification, especially when investors want to balance traditional fixed income with the backing of a real asset.
Inflation-Indexed Bonds (IIBs)
These bonds are structured to deal with inflation. Both the principal and interest are adjusted based on inflation levels. So over time, the real value of returns stays intact. Many times, these are considered when the focus is not just earning returns but maintaining purchasing power.
Bonds with Call or Put Option
These come with built-in flexibility. The government can choose to buy back the bond early, or the investor can exit under specific conditions. In practice, this feature becomes relevant when interest rate cycles shift and either side wants to adjust their position.
Zero-Coupon Bonds
These do not pay periodic interest. Instead, they are issued at a lower price and redeemed at face value. The return comes at maturity.

Category: bonds

[Government bonds in India](https://altifi.ai/bonds/government-securities) are debt instruments issued by the Central and State Governments to raise funds for public spending. These are used in areas such as infrastructure development, welfare schemes, and fiscal management. In simple terms, when you invest in a government bond, you are lending funds to the government in return for periodic interest payments and repayment of the principal at maturity. There are many types of government bonds in India. This article explores the different types of government bonds in India.
What are Government Bonds?
Government bonds, or Government Securities in India, are essentially a way for the government to borrow funds from investors. You lend to the government for a fixed period, usually anywhere between 5 and 40 years, and in return, you receive interest at regular intervals along with the principal at maturity.
In practice, these instruments sit at the stable end of the investment spectrum. The sovereign backing makes them highly reliable, which is why many investors use them as a foundation in their portfolio rather than as a growth driver.
Different Types of Government Bonds in India
Once you move beyond the basic definition, the structure starts to vary. Each type of bond is designed with a slightly different purpose in mind.
Fixed-Rate Bonds
These are relatively straightforward. The interest rate stays the same throughout the tenure. Basically, what you see at the start is what you continue to receive. Investors who want clarity in cash flows may prefer these.
Floating Rate Bonds (FRBs)
Here, the interest rate does not stay fixed. It resets at predefined intervals and is usually linked to a benchmark. Worth noting, these tend to work better when interest rates are moving up, since the returns adjust along with the market.
Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs)
They allowing investing in gold without dealing with physical storage. You get returns linked to gold prices along with a fixed interest component. In practice, this makes them useful for diversification, especially when investors want to balance traditional fixed income with the backing of a real asset.
Inflation-Indexed Bonds (IIBs)
These bonds are structured to deal with inflation. Both the principal and interest are adjusted based on inflation levels. So over time, the real value of returns stays intact. Many times, these are considered when the focus is not just earning returns but maintaining purchasing power.
Bonds with Call or Put Option
These come with built-in flexibility. The government can choose to buy back the bond early, or the investor can exit under specific conditions. In practice, this feature becomes relevant when interest rate cycles shift and either side wants to adjust their position.
Zero-Coupon Bonds
These do not pay periodic interest. Instead, they are issued at a lower price and redeemed at face value. The return comes at maturity.

State Development Loans (SDLs)
Issued by state governments, these work very similarly to central government bonds. They may offer relatively better yields. Worth noting, many investors use them to potentially enhance the returns while staying within a relatively stable category.
Advantages of Government Bonds
From a practical standpoint, a few things stand out:
- Strong reliability due to sovereign backing
- Relaively stable income in many cases
- May help balance overall portfolio risk
- May be used for portfolio diversification
- Certain types may help manage inflation impact
Disadvantages of Government Bonds
At the same time, there are trade-offs:
- Returns are relatively lower compared to market-linked instruments
- Fixed structures may not keep pace with rising inflation
- Longer tenures require patience and planning
The Process Involved in Government Bonds
At a basic level, the process is quite simple:
- You lend funds to the government
- You receive interest at regular intervals
- The principal is returned at maturity
- The funds are used for public spending and development
Who Should Consider Government Bonds?
In practice, these may suit:
- Investors who prefer stability over volatility
- Those looking for steady income
- Long-term planners, especially for retirement
- Anyone trying to bring balance to a portfolio with mixed assets
Conclusion
Government bonds in India are not just about safety, they are about structure and purpose. They may offer a reliable way to enhance stability into a portfolio. The different types, whether fixed-rate, floating, inflation-linked, or gold-based, are often used by the Indian government for various purposes. Each type caters to a slightly different need, and that is where their practical value lies.
FAQs on Government Bonds in India
How can an individual start investing in government bonds?
You can invest through RBI Retail Direct, banks, or brokerage platforms that offer access to government securities.
Do government bonds lose value before maturity?
Yes, their market price can fluctuate with interest rate changes if traded before maturity.
Which type of government bond helps during rising inflation?
Inflation-indexed bonds are specifically structured to adjust returns based on inflation levels.
Are sovereign gold bonds better than physical gold?
They remove storage concerns and add periodic interest, which many investors find more efficient in practice.
What is the typical holding period for these bonds?
Most government bonds are long-term, often starting from 5 years and extending up to 40 years.

title: Barbell, Bullet & Ladder Bond Strategies Explained
content:
Bond investment strategies help investors organise bond investments based on maturity, cash flow requirements, and interest rate expectations. Among the commonly used approaches are the barbell, bullet, and ladder strategies, each following a different way of selecting bond maturities. The choice of strategy depends on factors such as investment objectives, time horizon, liquidity needs, and risk considerations. Understanding how these approaches work makes it easier to compare them and identify which one aligns with a particular investment plan.
Understanding Bond Investment Strategies
A bond investment strategy is a structured approach to selecting and managing bonds with different maturities. Instead of purchasing bonds randomly, investors follow a planned method based on their financial objectives, investment horizon, and cash flow requirements.
Different strategies focus on different maturity patterns. Some concentrate investments around a single maturity date, while others spread investments across multiple tenures. Certain strategies also combine short-term and long-term bonds to create a diversified maturity profile.
The objective of these strategies is to manage interest rate risk, reinvestment risk, and liquidity according to individual investment requirements. No single strategy is suitable for every situation, which is why understanding each approach is important before making investment decisions.
Barbell, Bullet & Ladder Strategies at a Glance
Barbell, bullet and ladder are three commonly used bond investment strategies that differ mainly in how bond maturities are arranged within a portfolio. The barbell strategy combines short-term and long-term bonds, the bullet strategy focuses on bonds with a similar maturity period, and the ladder strategy spreads investments across multiple maturities. Each approach follows a different maturity structure and is designed to address investment planning, liquidity requirements, and reinvestment opportunities in different ways.
Barbell Bond Strategy
The barbell bond strategy involves investing in two ends of the maturity spectrum. A portion of the portfolio is allocated to short-term bonds, while the remaining portion is invested in long-term bonds. Medium-term bonds generally receive little or no allocation.
Short-term bonds mature earlier, allowing investors to access funds or reinvest them as interest rates change. Long-term bonds remain invested for a longer duration and continue generating coupon payments over their tenure.
The following are the main features of the barbell bond strategy.
- Investments are divided between short-term and long-term bonds.
- Medium-term bonds generally have limited allocation.
- Short-term bonds mature earlier and provide periodic reinvestment opportunities.
- Long-term bonds remain invested over a longer period.
- The portfolio includes bonds with different interest rate sensitivities.
Bullet Bond Strategy
The bullet bond strategy focuses on purchasing bonds that mature around the same time. Investors gradually build a portfolio where most bonds have a common maturity year, even if they are purchased at different times.
This approach is generally used when funds may be required for a planned financial objective at a specific future date, such as buying a house, retirement, or education.

title: Barbell, Bullet & Ladder Bond Strategies Explained
content:
Bullet Bond Strategy
The bullet bond strategy focuses on purchasing bonds that mature around the same time. Investors gradually build a portfolio where most bonds have a common maturity year, even if they are purchased at different times.
This approach is generally used when funds may be required for a planned financial objective at a specific future date, such as buying a house, retirement, or education. Since most bonds mature together, the principal becomes available during the selected period.
The following are the main features of the bullet bond strategy.
- Bonds are selected with similar maturity dates.
- Investments may be made over time while maintaining the target maturity.
- The portfolio is aligned with a specific investment horizon.
- Principal from multiple bonds becomes available around the same period.
- The strategy focuses on a defined maturity objective.
Ladder Bond Strategy
The ladder bond strategy involves investing in bonds with different maturity periods. Instead of concentrating investments in one tenure, the portfolio is spread across short-term, medium-term, and long-term bonds.
As each bond matures, the proceeds are commonly reinvested into a new long-term bond, maintaining the maturity ladder over time. This creates staggered maturity dates across the portfolio.
The following are the main features of the ladder bond strategy.
- Investments are spread across multiple maturities.
- Bonds mature at regular intervals.
- Helps maintain a balance between liquidity and longer-term bond exposure through staggered maturity dates.
- Matured proceeds may be reinvested into new long-term bonds.
- The portfolio maintains exposure across different tenures.
- Reinvestment takes place periodically instead of all at once.
Comparison: Barbell vs Bullet vs Ladder Strategy
The following table compares the bullet ladder and barbell strategies across important parameters.
| Parameter | Barbell Strategy | Bullet Strategy | Ladder Strategy | 
| Maturity Structure | Short-term (1 to 3 years) and long-term (7 to 10 years) maturities with limited exposure to medium-term bonds | Similar maturity dates | Diverse maturity periods such as 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 10 years | 
| Investment Approach | Invests in short-term and long-term bonds | Invests in bonds maturing around the same period | Invests across multiple maturity periods | 
| Medium-Term Exposure | Limited or no exposure to medium-term bonds | Depends on target maturity | Included | 
| Liquidity | Higher from short-term allocation | Mostly available at target maturity | Available at regular intervals | 
| Reinvestment Frequency | Periodic through short-term maturities | Mostly at final maturity | Regular as bonds mature | 
| Common Objective | Ample liquidity with short-term bonds exposure | Aligns investments with a future financial requirement | Creates regular maturity intervals, reinvestment opportunities, and liquidity balance | 
Advantages and Limitations of Each Strategy

Factors to Consider Before Choosing a Bond Strategy
The following are some factors investors may consider before selecting a bond strategy.
Investment Objective
Investors should assess their investment objective by identifying their financial goal, such as generating regular cash flows or planning for a future expense. Having clarity about the objective may help in selecting an appropriate bond strategy.
Investment Horizon
Investors may consider how long they intend to remain invested. The investment horizon may influence whether a strategy with short-term, long-term, or staggered bond maturities is more suitable.
Liquidity Requirement
Investors may evaluate when they are likely to require access to their funds. This assessment may help determine whether regular bond maturities or a single maturity period closely align with their liquidity needs.
Interest Rate Environment
Investors may review the prevailing interest rate environment, as changes in interest rates may affect bond prices and reinvestment opportunities. This may influence the maturity structure chosen for the portfolio.
Risk Tolerance
Investors may assess their willingness to accept fluctuations in bond prices and reinvestment risk. Understanding risk tolerance may help in selecting a strategy that aligns with their investment approach.
Cash Flow Requirement
Investors should consider whether they require funds at regular intervals or around a specific future date. This may help determine the maturity pattern that effectively supports their cash flow requirements.
Portfolio Allocation
Investors may review their existing investment portfolio before selecting a bond strategy. The current asset allocation may influence how bond investments are distributed across different maturities.

The choice of bond strategy depends on the investment objective, time horizon, liquidity requirement, and overall portfolio structure rather than on a single factor.

title: Bullet Bonds Explained: Benefits, Risks and How They Work
content:
Bullet bonds are a type of debt instrument where the entire principal is repaid in one lump sum at maturity, rather than instalments. This makes them a unique type of bonds and are categorised as non-amortising bonds. Investors generally consider such instruments as a source of regular income. In this blog, let’s explore bullet bonds in detail and also understand how they differ from amortising bonds which repay the prinicipal over the bond’s tenure.
Understanding Bullet Bonds
A bullet bond is a debt instrument in which the issuer repays the full face value to the bondholder in one lump sum on the maturity date. No part of the principal is repaid before then, which makes the structure different from an amortising bond where principal is returned gradually over the tenure. During the bond’s tenure, investors typically receive coupon payments at fixed intervals, such as quarterly, semi-annually, or annually, depending on the bond’s terms.
For example, if an investor buys a 5-year bullet bond with a face value of ₹1,00,000 and an annual coupon rate of 8%, the investor may receive ₹8,000 as coupon income each year. However, the ₹1,00,000 principal will be repaid only at the end of the fifth year, provided the issuer meets its repayment obligations. This structure helps investors estimate expected cash flows, while issuers benefit from retaining the borrowed amount for the full tenure.
Bullet bonds may be useful for investors who want regular interest income and are comfortable waiting until maturity to receive the principal. However, it places a larger repayment obligation on the issuer at the end of the bond’s tenure. So, investors must properly assess the refinancing and credit risks before investing.
Why Do Companies Issue Bullet Bonds?
Companies may issue bullet bonds for several common reasons.
Cash Flow Management During the Tenure
By deferring principal repayment until maturity, the issuing company can use the full capital throughout the bond’s tenure. This is especially useful for capital-intensive sectors such as infrastructure, real estate, and power generation, where project cash flows may materialise only after several years.
Refinancing Flexibility
Bullet bonds can give issuers flexibility to refinance at maturity. If interest rates are lower when the bond matures, the company may repay existing bondholders and raise new capital at a potentially lower cost.
Alignment with Market Conventions
In India, SEBI regulates listed corporate bonds under its applicable regulations. The bullet repayment structure is consistent with common market practice for listed Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs), Government Securities (G-Secs), and Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) bonds.
Institutional Demand
Institutional investors such as mutual funds, insurance companies, and pension funds often allocate to bullet bonds.

No part of the principal is repaid before then, which makes the structure different from an amortising bond where principal is returned gradually over the tenure. During the bond’s tenure, investors typically receive coupon payments at fixed intervals, such as quarterly, semi-annually, or annually, depending on the bond’s terms.
For example, if an investor buys a 5-year bullet bond with a face value of ₹1,00,000 and an annual coupon rate of 8%, the investor may receive ₹8,000 as coupon income each year. However, the ₹1,00,000 principal will be repaid only at the end of the fifth year, provided the issuer meets its repayment obligations. This structure helps investors estimate expected cash flows, while issuers benefit from retaining the borrowed amount for the full tenure.
Bullet bonds may be useful for investors who want regular interest income and are comfortable waiting until maturity to receive the principal. However, it places a larger repayment obligation on the issuer at the end of the bond’s tenure. So, investors must properly assess the refinancing and credit risks before investing.
Why Do Companies Issue Bullet Bonds?
Companies may issue bullet bonds for several common reasons.
Cash Flow Management During the Tenure
By deferring principal repayment until maturity, the issuing company can use the full capital throughout the bond’s tenure. This is especially useful for capital-intensive sectors such as infrastructure, real estate, and power generation, where project cash flows may materialise only after several years.
Refinancing Flexibility
Bullet bonds can give issuers flexibility to refinance at maturity. If interest rates are lower when the bond matures, the company may repay existing bondholders and raise new capital at a potentially lower cost.
Alignment with Market Conventions
In India, SEBI regulates listed corporate bonds under its applicable regulations. The bullet repayment structure is consistent with common market practice for listed Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs), Government Securities (G-Secs), and Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) bonds.
Institutional Demand
Institutional investors such as mutual funds, insurance companies, and pension funds often allocate to bullet bonds.

FAQs About Bullet Bonds
What is a bullet bond?
A bullet bond is a debt instrument where the full principal is returned as a single lump sum on the maturity date, with periodic coupon payments made during the tenure.
How is a bullet bond different from an amortising bond?
In an amortising bond, principal and interest are repaid in regular instalments. In a bullet bond, only coupon payments are made periodically; the full principal is returned at maturity.
What is refinancing risk in bullet bonds?
Refinancing risk is the possibility that the issuer may not be able to arrange funds to repay the full principal at maturity, which may lead to delayed payments or default.
Are bullet bonds listed on Indian stock exchanges?
Many bullet bonds issued by companies in India may be listed on the NSE or BSE, though secondary market liquidity may vary depending on the specific bond.
How is coupon income from bullet bonds taxed in India?
Coupon payments are taxable under "Income from Other Sources" at the applicable slab rate.

What is the typical tenure of bullet bonds in India?
Bullet bonds in India may have a tenure ranging from 1 to 10 years, with some issuances extending to 15 or 20 years, depending on the issuer's requirements.

title: What are Government Bonds
content:
Government bonds are debt instruments issued by the government to finance various expenditures such as public spending or constructing various projects. Such securities are issued by either the Government of India or the respective states' governments. The interest payment made periodically by the borrower is called coupons. Government bonds are generally considered to be an integral part of fixed-income investments.
The process of issuing the bonds takes place either through auction or an issuance program. They are usually affected by changes in interest rates, inflation, and the economy. For many investors, they form a structured component of debt allocation within a portfolio.
How Government Bonds Work
Government bonds function through a simple flow of issuance, investment, and repayment.
The government issues a bond with a defined face value, coupon rate, and maturity period. Investors subscribe to these bonds either in the primary issuance or through the secondary market. Once purchased, the issuer may pay interest at regular intervals, depending on the bond structure.
At maturity, the principal amount is repaid to the investor. In some cases, bond prices may fluctuate in the secondary market before maturity due to interest rate changes and market demand conditions.
Types of Government Bonds
Government bonds come in different structures designed to suit varied investor needs and market conditions. These instruments differ based on interest rate design, maturity structure, and optional features.
Bonds with Call or Put Option
These bonds come with embedded options that allow either the issuer or the investor to act before maturity under specific conditions. A call option enables the issuer to redeem the bond early, usually when government bonds interest rates fall. A put option allows the investor to exit early under defined terms. These features introduce flexibility but may also affect income stability and holding duration expectations.
Fixed-Rate Government Bonds
Fixed-rate government bonds carry a predetermined coupon rate throughout the tenure. The interest remains constant regardless of market fluctuations. This structure allows investors to estimate periodic income more clearly. However, overall changes in government bond interest rates may influence the market value of these bonds in the secondary market.
Floating Rate Bonds
Floating rate bonds have variable coupon payments linked to a benchmark rate, which is reset periodically. This means interest income may adjust over time depending on market rate movements. These instruments are often used in changing interest rate environments, where fixed-income structures may not fully reflect market conditions.
Inflation-Indexed Bonds
Inflation-linked bonds have been designed in such a way that they offer returns tied to the level of inflation. The principal or interest payment is indexed according to inflation indices. This arrangement has been devised to ensure that the value of money is maintained over time despite any variations in actual returns.
Zero-Coupon Bonds
Zero-coupon bonds do not pay periodic interest. Instead, they are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value on maturity. The difference between the purchase price and the maturity value represents the return. These instruments are often used for long-term planning needs where cash flows are not required during the holding period.

Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs)
[Sovereign Gold Bonds](https://altifi.ai/bonds/sovereign-gold-bond) are issued by the Government of India and are linked to gold prices. Advantages and Disadvantages of Investing in Government Bonds
Government bonds offer several features that may appeal to different investor profiles, although they also come with certain limitations.
| Advantages | Disadvantages | 
|---|---|
| Regular coupon payments may provide steady income visibility | Returns may be influenced by interest rate movements | 
| Issued by sovereign entities, historically associated with lower credit risk | Market value may fluctuate in the secondary market | 
| Useful for portfolio diversification across asset classes | Inflation may affect real return over time | 
| Available in multiple structures to suit different needs | Liquidity may vary depending on bond type | 
| Transparent regulatory framework under SEBI and RBI guidelines | Long duration bonds may be sensitive to rate changes | 
Who Can Consider Investing in Government Bonds
Government bonds may suit different types of investors depending on financial goals and risk profile.
- New Investors: People exploring fixed-income instruments as an alternative to traditional savings products may find these bonds useful.
- Retail Investors: Investors who want to reduce their equity holdings by diversifying into government bonds may use these instruments.
- Income-focused Investors: Those seeking periodic coupon income may include these instruments for planned cash flow needs.
- Long-term Planners: Investors with defined future financial goals may use bonds with specific maturities.
- HNI Investors: High-net-worth individuals may use government bonds for portfolio structuring and duration management.
- Financial Intermediaries: Advisors and distributors may use these instruments for client portfolio allocation across risk profiles.
Conclusion
Government bonds are a type of popular debt instrument which enables participants to engage in structured loans to the government. They come in various types, such as fixed, floating, inflation, and gold-linked forms, which can fit certain investment requirements. These financial instruments react to changes in interest rates, inflation, and market demand conditions. They may be included in investment strategies due to their ability to contribute to portfolio diversification.
FAQs
Are government bonds and Government Securities (G-Secs) the same?
Government Securities (G-Secs) is a broader category that includes government bonds.

title: Market Linked Debentures (MLDs): Meaning, Types & Risks
content:
Market Linked Debentures (MLDs) form part of the structured debt segment within the fixed-income market. These instruments differ from conventional bonds in terms of structure, payout mechanism, and market linkage. They are typically considered by individuals who are exploring alternatives beyond traditional fixed-income products such as fixed deposits and standard debt securities. MLDs are designed to offer exposure to underlying market indices while retaining certain features of debt instruments. Understanding their basic structure and characteristics is often the first step in evaluating their role within a broader investment portfolio.
What are Market Linked Debentures (MLDs)?
A Market Linked Debenture is a structured debt instrument where the final payout depends on the performance of an underlying market benchmark. Unlike standard bonds that pay a fixed coupon rate, MLDs tie returns to market benchmarks such as the Nifty 50, government security yields, or gold prices. The investor receives a lump sum at maturity rather than periodic interest payments, which is a key distinction from regular NCDs that pay coupons quarterly or annually.
MLDs fall under SEBI's Non-Convertible Securities (NCS) Regulations, 2021. They are classified as non-convertible debentures with an embedded derivative component. This means the issuer combines a traditional debt obligation with a market-linked payoff formula.
Typical issuers include NBFCs, investment banks, and large financial institutions. These entities use MLDs to raise capital while offering individuals exposure to market movements without direct equity ownership.
How Do MLDs Work?
Every MLD is built around two components that work together to determine the final payout.
Component 1: The Debt Component
This is the foundation. The issuer takes the invested amount and allocates a portion to a zero-coupon bond or similar debt instrument. This component is designed to return the principal at maturity. In a principal-protected MLD (PP-MLD), where the principal amount is intended to be returned at maturity, the debt allocation covers 100% of the face value at maturity, subject to issuer credit risk.
For example, if an investor puts in Rs 10,00,000 in a 3-year PP-MLD, the issuer might allocate roughly Rs 8,50,000 to a zero-coupon bond yielding enough to accumulate to Rs 10,00,000 over three years. The remaining Rs 1,50,000 funds the second component.
Component 2: The Derivative Component
This is where the market-linked return comes from. The issuer uses the remaining funds to purchase options or other derivative contracts tied to the chosen benchmark. The participation rate determines how much of its movement the investor actually captures.
A participation rate of 80% means the investor receives 80% upside.

title: Market Linked Debentures (MLDs): Meaning, Types & Risks
content:
Component 2: The Derivative Component
This is where the market-linked return comes from. The issuer uses the remaining funds to purchase options or other derivative contracts tied to the chosen benchmark. The participation rate determines how much of its movement the investor actually captures.
A participation rate of 80% means the investor receives 80% upside. If the Nifty 50 rises 25% over the MLD tenure, the market-linked return would be 80% × 25% = 20% on the face value.
For Instance:
Consider an investor who purchases a 3-year PP-MLD with a face value of Rs 10,00,000. The underlying benchmark is the Nifty 50, and the participation rate is 80%.
Scenario A: Nifty rises 25%:
MLD Return = Rs 10,00,000 × 80% × 25% = Rs 2,00,000
Total payout at maturity = Rs 12,00,000
Scenario B: Nifty falls 10%:
Because this is a principal-protected MLD, the investor receives Rs 10,00,000 back. The derivative component expires worthless, but the debt component covers the principal.
This two-part design is why MLDs behave differently from both plain bonds and equity investments. The debt component handles capital preservation while the derivative component aims for potential gains.
Types of Market Linked Debentures
The following are the two primary structural types of MLDs available in India.
Principal-Protected MLDs
In a PP-MLD, the issuing company allocates a sufficient portion of the invested amount to a debt instrument so that the face value is returned at maturity. The investor's downside, in terms of market performance, is limited to receiving zero market-linked return. The original capital, however, comes back.
Historically, MLDs were primarily accessible to high-net-worth individuals because of higher minimum investment requirements. However, the minimum investment threshold for many MLD issuances has reduced to around ₹1 lakh, making these instruments more accessible to a wider range of individuals.
Non-Principal-Protected MLDs
Non-PP MLDs usually do not offer protection of the invested principal. If the benchmark moves against the investor's position, the payout at maturity may be less than the amount originally invested. These structures typically offer higher participation rates or more aggressive market exposure in exchange for this capital risk.
Non-PP MLDs are generally considered more suitable for experienced individuals who have a clear understanding of derivative payoff structures and are comfortable with the possibility of receiving less than the invested amount.
Key Features of MLDs

MLD Return = Rs 10,00,000 × 80% × 25% = Rs 2,00,000
Total payout at maturity = Rs 12,00,000
Scenario B: Nifty falls 10%:
Because this is a principal-protected MLD, the investor receives Rs 10,00,000 back. The derivative component expires worthless, but the debt component covers the principal.
This two-part design is why MLDs behave differently from both plain bonds and equity investments. The debt component handles capital preservation while the derivative component aims for potential gains.
Types of Market Linked Debentures
The following are the two primary structural types of MLDs available in India.
Principal-Protected MLDs
In a PP-MLD, the issuing company allocates a sufficient portion of the invested amount to a debt instrument so that the face value is returned at maturity. The investor's downside, in terms of market performance, is limited to receiving zero market-linked return. The original capital, however, comes back.
Historically, MLDs were primarily accessible to high-net-worth individuals because of higher minimum investment requirements. However, the minimum investment threshold for many MLD issuances has reduced to around ₹1 lakh, making these instruments more accessible to a wider range of individuals.
Non-Principal-Protected MLDs
Non-PP MLDs usually do not offer protection of the invested principal. If the benchmark moves against the investor's position, the payout at maturity may be less than the amount originally invested. These structures typically offer higher participation rates or more aggressive market exposure in exchange for this capital risk.
Non-PP MLDs are generally considered more suitable for experienced individuals who have a clear understanding of derivative payoff structures and are comfortable with the possibility of receiving less than the invested amount.
Key Features of MLDs

Key Features of MLDs
The following are a few key features that distinguish MLDs from other fixed-income instruments.
Market-Linked Returns
MLD returns are not fixed at issuance. The payout depends on the performance of the underlying benchmark between the investment date and the maturity date. The point-to-point method is the most common calculation approach used in Indian MLD issuances, where only the benchmark value at the start and the value at maturity are considered. Interim movements do not affect the final calculation.
Fixed Tenure
MLDs are issued with a defined tenure, typically ranging from one to five years. The tenure is set at issuance and usually does not change. Secondary market liquidity in these instruments tends to be limited, which may result in positions remaining untraded until maturity.
Principal Protection
Not all MLDs offer principal protection. In a Principal-Protected MLD (PP-MLD), the debt component is structured to return the face value at maturity regardless of how the benchmark performs. In a Non-Principal-Protected MLD (Non-PP MLD), the investor's capital may be at risk if it moves unfavourably.
What Determines MLD Returns?
MLD returns are generally determined by three key variables set at the time of issuance i.e. the chosen benchmark, the participation rate, and the tenure.
| Benchmark | Return Driver | Typical Rationale | 
| Gold Price | Movement in domestic or international gold prices | Provides exposure to gold price movements without holding physical gold. | 
| Government Bond Yield (10-year G-Sec) | Movement in government bond yields | Offers exposure to interest rate movements and bond market trends. | 
| Nifty 50 / Sensex | Broad Indian equity market performance | Provides exposure to the performance of large-cap equities through a structured debt instrument. | 
| Nifty Midcap 150 / Small-cap Indices | Performance of mid-cap or small-cap equities | Offers exposure to segments of the equity market that may experience higher volatility and return potential. | 
| Multi-asset or Custom Basket | Performance of a combination of benchmarks | Provides diversified exposure across multiple asset classes or market indicators. | 
Benefits of Investing in MLDs
The following are a few potential benefits that individuals may consider when evaluating MLDs.
- MLDs may offer market-linked upside through a debt instrument structure, without directly holding equity.
- PP-MLDs may provide a defined floor on principal return, which may be relevant for individuals seeking some degree of capital preservation alongside market exposure.
